section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Novel structures, design criteria, and drainage intensity
claim_paragraph: Many site studies conclude that established design criteria require re-evaluation. New criteria protecting crops while minimising drain-water salinity and volume are sought \parencite{Christen2001}, along with updated depths and spacings at specific sites \parencite{Muhammad2021,Malota2016,Bahçeci2009,Kahlown2002}, review of recommended spacings paired with controlled-traffic farming \parencite{Mante2022,Mante2018}, cost-effectiveness of narrow spacings in claypan soils \parencite{Nelson2017}, and standard depth-and-spacing guidelines tested in situ before extension \parencite{HajAmor2019}. Design should account for changing crop water needs, climate, and irrigation modernisation **[CITATION CHECKED: Akram2013]**, and design intensity itself is an open question: reduced spacing would require increased network capacity and heighten reliance on best management practices \parencite{Singh2009,Dialameh2025}, a systems approach should integrate drainage, crop--soil processes, and nutrient-loss reduction \parencite{Castellano2019}, and DRAINMOD-based analysis should develop optimum rates and spacings across locations \parencite{Strock2011}. Which soil parameters are most critical, and what confidence intervals each requires, remain fundamental questions \parencite{Ayars2015,SHIRMOHAMMADI1995,HARDJOAMIDJOJO1982}. Design guidance must rest on long records: drainage design should not rely on short-term simulations \parencite{Wang2006b}, and long runs with hourly input are needed to assess wider spacings, interannual variability, and shallow-water-table control \parencite{Ale2009,Häggblom2019,Malota2015,Salo2019,Kladivko2023,Chang2012}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Controlled drainage, subirrigation, and drainage water management
claim_paragraph: Automation and data-driven control are identified as the next technological step. \textcite{Youssef2023} call for a new generation of control structures and decision-support tools, sensor-based systems for shallow-water-table soils, and systems that adapt to changing weather, and **[CITATION CHECKED: Ayars2015]** for adaptive-control decision support. Concrete agendas include dynamic modelling and data assimilation of the field water balance, feasible control-problem formulations, and fusion of control automation with physical infrastructure \parencite{Ikonen2023,Isomäki2024}, automatic water-depth control for aerobic rice \parencite{Arif2021}, and earlier farm decision aids incorporating quantity, quality, crop growth, and economics \parencite{THOMAS1995}. Coordinating irrigation with drainage control is a persistent problem: irrigation must be reduced when CD is implemented, requiring coordination among authorities and farmers \parencite{Wahba2005,Ritzema2011,Ritzema2016}, and CD requires genuinely integrated management with careful site selection \parencite{Dukhovny2018}. Subirrigation embedded in regional water systems is a distinct, largely unresolved frontier: regional water needs should be known before responsible incorporation, with optimised pumping and cautious use of alternative resources \parencite{deWit2022}, and SWAP-type modelling can pre-screen sites and forecast consequences before implementation \parencite{deWit2024}. Seepage effects on CD performance need coordinated experimental and modelling research, including guard lines to evaluate lateral seepage \parencite{Youssef2021,Pease2017,Ale2009}, and excess-moisture stress, spring drawdown, and spring nitrogen loading are priorities \parencite{Craft2018,Lahdou2019}. Anticipatory, forecast-based management should incorporate evapotranspiration, subirrigation, and spatially variable seepage and address forecast uncertainty \parencite{VandeCraats2021}, collector-ditch water-level and control schedules should be optimised \parencite{Salla2022,Strock2025b}, and CD should be paired with local crop and climate characteristics without overlooking rapid water-table decrease raising irrigation demand in dry summers \parencite{Güngör2023,Dou2023,Golmohammadi2016,Kim2023,Wang2020c}. Longer-term studies must disentangle whether soil-property changes under drainage--subirrigation arise from the practice or from irrigation-water quality \parencite{Kaur2023}, and complete water and nutrient budgets within and across field boundaries, plus effects on runoff, preferential flow, and recharge, remain to be tracked \parencite{Shedekar2021,Ross2016,King2022}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: From field to watershed: scaling, routing, and connectivity
claim_paragraph: A defining open problem is the disconnect between field-scale process knowledge and watershed-scale response. Quantifying the relationships between field processes and watershed response is repeatedly identified as a critical need for water-quality strategy, with explicit field-to-watershed linkage and upscaling frameworks \parencite{Williams2015,Williams2017,Wang2020b}. Small, intensively monitored catchments are proposed as the empirical bridge for upscaling and model validation **[CITATION CHECKED: Basu2010]**, and effectiveness estimates for drainage water management and phosphorus mitigation should be scaled up from field to watershed \parencite{Wang2021,Ross2016,Shedekar2021}. The hydrologic effects of tiling remain inadequately characterised at watershed scale and must be pursued through combined modelling and field data---attending to seasonal streamflow recessions in tiled versus non-tiled watersheds \parencite{Schilling2008,Schilling2012}, events of all sizes across landscapes \parencite{Sloan2017}, routing between spatially variable depressional stores and flow accumulation across river networks \parencite{Sloan2016,Fonley2021}, and the decoupling of row-crop cover from artificial drainage and of surface from subsurface contributions \parencite{BolandBrien2014}. Interactions between drains and the receiving channel network are a frontier in their own right: the fate and transport of tile effluent after it reaches surface drains \parencite{Clement2017}, drain--river/ditch interactions \parencite{Grangeon2021}, and field-scale monitoring of tile flow's impact on downstream discharge, stream power, and channel geomorphology \parencite{Zhou2025,Zhou2013}. Streamflow prediction in tiled landscapes remains difficult, raising the question of whether curve-number or more process-based methods are required \parencite{Wessel2022,Thomas2016,Rahman2014}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Uncertainty, experimental design, and integrative frameworks
claim_paragraph: A final cross-cutting frontier is methodological integration. \textcite{Dollinger2015} articulate the most explicit long-range vision: numerically explicit landscape-scale models that couple the processes governing ditch services, optimise the spatial arrangement of practices according to connectivity, and define multi-service maximisation strategies informed by stakeholder-valued rankings, prerequisite to which is better mapping of ditch hydraulic, vegetation, and sorption properties \parencite{Dollinger2015,Herzon2008}. Landscape-scale integrated approaches combining on-farm change with off-site wetland and riparian restoration are broadly endorsed **[CITATION CHECKED: Blann2009]**, and truly integrated watershed management requires better information on controlling processes such as groundwater-head distribution linking topography--geology to the drain fraction \parencite{Mahmood2023}. Coupled field--watershed models enable water-table- management scenario analyses not possible with component models used separately \parencite{Dayyani2010}, frameworks should remain extensible to additional processes and dynamically calibrated indices \parencite{Basu2010,Tao2025,Verma2014}, and modelling should increasingly guide practice placement and stacking \parencite{Kröger2013,Tomer2015,Lemke2011,McDowell2021,King2022,Roley2016}. Adapting drainage design to a changing climate is an explicit priority, tied to understanding weather--soil--groundwater--discharge interactions under increased precipitation and to model assessment over longer periods and different climates \parencite{Deelstra2015,Tuohy2018,Malota2024,Deelstra2014,Deelstra2014b}. Coupled process representations---water-vapour and heat--water flow in dry soils, density-driven and hydrobiogeochemical solute transport, and winter runoff and sediment indicators---round out the frontier \parencite{Moroizumi2004,Koivusalo1999,Salo2015,Varvaris2018,Augeard2005}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: A striking feature of the subsurface (tile) drainage literature is that its most confident statements are about what remains unknown. Across humid temperate cropland, arid and semi-arid irrigated plains, saline coastal soils, and tropical oases, authors converge on a shared diagnosis: theory, models, and management hypotheses have outrun the field evidence available to test them. Process representations remain untested outside the conditions in which they were built; model parameters cannot be constrained without measurements that were never made; and management practices are recommended on the strength of short records at single sites. The research frontier is therefore defined less by a shortage of ideas than by a shortage of the right data at the right spatial and temporal resolution to calibrate, validate, and generalise. This section organises the open questions, hypotheses, and methodological needs that recur throughout the literature into a small set of interlocking themes. First, process-based drainage and water-quality models (DRAINMOD and its derivatives, SWAT, APEX, RZWQM2, HYDRUS, MIKE~SHE, CRHM, WEPP, and numerous salinity codes) are repeatedly flagged as requiring rigorous independent testing, with particular weaknesses in phosphorus, macropore and preferential-flow, sediment, and seepage components \parencite{Youssef2006,Askar2021b,Askar2025,Radcliffe2015,Williams2016}. Second, the physical processes that most strongly govern drain hydrographs---preferential and macropore flow, spatially and temporally variable soil hydraulic properties, and the coupling among soil pore-water flow, pipe flow, and surface water---remain incompletely characterised. Third, the location, extent, and specifications of drainage networks are largely unknown, motivating remote-sensing, geophysical, and database efforts. Fourth, scaling from well-instrumented fields to the watersheds where water-quality goals are set is an unresolved methodological problem. Fifth, active management strategies---controlled drainage, subirrigation, drainage water recycling, and edge-of-field treatment---lack the coordinated field-and-simulation programmes needed to quantify their trade-offs. Sixth, salt leaching, drainage-water reuse, and disposal remain only partially understood and only partially observable. Finally, a persistent methodological agenda spans uncertainty quantification, experimental design, long-term monitoring, economics, and the institutional context of adoption. A cross-cutting message unites them: the binding constraint is coordinated, long-term, year-round data, and progress requires improved process representation and improved field verification to advance together rather than separately **[CITATION CHECKED: Frankenberger2024]**.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Salt leaching, drainage-water reuse, and disposal
claim_paragraph: Removing salt from soil relocates the problem to the drainage water, whose management is among the most persistent challenges. Environmentally acceptable disposal methods are needed \parencite{Ayars2014,Steppuhn2006}, evaporation-pond management must be tested at full scale and combined with volume/contamination reduction \parencite{BRADFORD1991}, and trace-element fate---arsenic speciation and uranium recovery or removal---compounds the problem \parencite{Gao2007,Duff1997,Gao2003}. Emerging treatment routes are at the demonstration stage: electrolysis of saline wastewater at varying salinity \parencite{Yang2023}, sorptive filter materials tested with real rather than artificial drainage water \parencite{Pugliese2023}, and blending of drainage and reverse-osmosis product water \parencite{Singh2020d}. Reuse-focused research spans site-specific load--flow relationships, germination-stage salinity tolerance, and improved scheduling that meets crop evapotranspiration from a shallow water table while minimising upward salt flow \parencite{WESTCOT1988}, provisional field guidance on substituting drainage water for wheat \parencite{Sharma1998}, blending and evaporation-pond storage \parencite{Datta2002}, farm-level reuse within a basin-wide salt balance \parencite{Qureshi2008}, seasonal groundwater undulation and drip conversion to prevent accumulation \parencite{Mirlas2021,Dou2022,Singh2019}, and biochar, phytoremediation, and reclamation innovations \parencite{Liu2025f,Steppuhn2017,Youngs2000}. Comprehensive assessment of waterlogging and salinity together, rather than separately, is recommended \parencite{Valipour2014}, and the economic feasibility of drainage as a preventive measure against salinisation remains to be established **[CITATION CHECKED: HalbacCotoaraZamfir2022]**.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Nutrient, carbon, and greenhouse-gas coupling
claim_paragraph: Improving the representation and understanding of nutrient transport---especially phosphorus---is a persistent priority. \textcite{King2015} call for enhanced phosphorus routines and simultaneous measurement of P losses in surface runoff and subsurface drainage to determine partitioning and avoid unintended consequences, and \textcite{Williams2016} stress differentiating soil versus fertiliser sources of tile-drained P. Additional needs include measuring the size distribution of particulate-P carriers \parencite{Qi2018}, determining which processes most reduce total-P loadings to drains \parencite{Geohring2001}, and retaining P at drain outlets \parencite{Zimmer2016}. Broader questions extend to nitrogen and receiving waters: P retention and uptake lengths and internal lake P loading \parencite{Clement2017}, individual and stacked practices to mitigate algal blooms \parencite{King2018}, cover crops, drainage water management, and 4R nutrient management targeting the non-growing season \parencite{King2016,Kokulan2021}, and legacy soil P interacting with hydrology in drained landscapes and closed depressions **[CITATION CHECKED: Hanrahan2020]**. At watershed scale, controlling surface runoff and tile flow with drainage-water-management devices and bioreactors, and strategies addressing both hydrology and nitrogen supply at district scale, are argued necessary for downstream benefit \parencite{Li2015,Ikenberry2014,Filipovic2015,BinShokrana2023,Koskiaho2002,Kladivko2005}. The full water-quality potential of controlled drainage and water-table management---across chemical fate, soil properties, and biological dynamics, plus a comprehensive solute-transport model---remains to be evaluated \parencite{FAUSEY1995,RITTER1995}, and dissolved-organic-carbon dynamics and their ecological implications are largely unknown \parencite{Ruark2009,Furukawa2008}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Transferability across soils, climates, crops, and management
claim_paragraph: A pervasive limitation is that findings from single sites or narrow conditions cannot yet be generalised. \textcite{Singh2022b} recommend that controlled-drainage and subirrigation studies be conducted outside the U.S.\ Midwest and Canada across diverse climates, crops, and soils, and that site characterisation---slope, particle-size distribution by horizon, hydraulic conductivity, drainage class, and moisture---be reported with measures of variability. Repetition at larger scales and on different soils is stressed as a key modulating factor \parencite{Bilotta2008,Goeken2015}, including earthworm studies on soils of different texture and rainfall \parencite{Nuutinen2001,Nuutinen2011}. Climate-focused transferability needs include high-resolution climate-change scenarios \parencite{Rasmussen2018}, multi-model uncertainty analysis at additional sites \parencite{Jeantet2022}, and drainage-warming and soil-texture effects on crops \parencite{Jin2008}. Crop- and practice-specific extensions are sought for paddy and trench drainage \parencite{Rahimi2024,Jia2023}, mole-drainage durability \parencite{JHA1995}, controlled-drainage principles for new regions \parencite{Sojka2020}, crop-rotation and tillage interactions \parencite{Ojeda2018}, and salt-flushing methods in heterogeneous soils \parencite{Yu2018}. Additional testing across regions, soils, and climates recurs throughout \parencite{Singh2020b,Malota2024,Salazar2008,Holbak2021}, and localised design methods reflecting local agro-technical conditions are called for **[CITATION CHECKED: He2002]**.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Locating, mapping, and cataloguing drainage networks
claim_paragraph: Because the physical drainage network is often unknown, uncertainty propagates into every downstream model, making detection and mapping a fast-moving frontier where methods work in some conditions but lack systematic guidelines. Actual tile locations and measured discharge would improve calibration \parencite{Amado2018}, and predictive mapping from imagery needs validation against GPS surveys and methods that avoid misidentifying noise and connect broken segments \parencite{Naz2009,Schilling2019}. The most explicit data agenda calls for reporting tile diameter, depth, spacing, and mains, and for a drainage database built jointly by agencies, researchers, landowners, and contractors, with repositories updated as data accrue \parencite{Zhou2025,Valayamkunnath2020}. Remote-sensing work seeks urgent development of non-invasive methods for aging systems, combining UAV flights with GPR \parencite{Wienken2024}, and multispectral, thermal-infrared, and machine-learning agendas that define the site conditions under which drain lines and outlets can be mapped, with decision-tree guidelines for practitioners \parencite{Allred2020,Allred2021,Allred2022}. \textcite{Carlsen2024} recommend reconsidering the often-cited 2.54~cm minimum rainfall for imagery acquisition, investigating deep learning, multitemporal acquisition, and synthetic aperture radar, and expanding public drainage-map datasets, echoed by calls for transformer-based architectures and higher-resolution imagery integrated into hydrologic frameworks \parencite{Wan2024}, and for reduced tracing uncertainty through multiple interpreters, ground truth, and richer covariates \parencite{Redoloza2023,Harris2018,Yimer2023}. Geophysical evaluations seek data from more sites and soils \parencite{Allred2005}, systematic testing of GPR antenna configuration and orientation \parencite{Allred2013}, prediction of GPR suitability via electromagnetic simulation from EMI, and concurrent EMI/GPR and drone/magnetic surveys with dependence on soil, residue, tillage, and wetness **[CITATION CHECKED: Jouen2018]**. Optical and radar covariate studies also seek more frequent imaging, repeated SAR with ground measurements, and UAV cover-crop mapping \parencite{Tlapáková2017,Meunier2001,Xu2018}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Coupled hydraulics, seepage, and soil heterogeneity
claim_paragraph: Closing the water balance---particularly seepage and groundwater exchange--- remains a persistent gap. Lateral seepage should be allowed to vary during simulation and included among inputs \parencite{Feng2018}, groundwater contributions could enter through double-storage or residual-storage models given hydrochemical data \parencite{DaneshYazdi2016}, and providing groundwater-table data in objective functions would sharpen inverse recovery of soil properties \parencite{Sedaghatdoost2018,Sedaghatdoost2019}. Improved calibration strategy is widely urged---parameter-estimation software and multiple conceptual models \parencite{Boico2022}, pilot-point distributed conductivity fields with soil-moisture observations and proxy machine-learning predictions \parencite{Schneider2022}, alternative objective functions such as Kling--Gupta efficiency \parencite{Brighenti2023}, and combined catchment--drainage-discharge calibration \parencite{DeSchepper2017}. Regional groundwater assessments call for radiocarbon sampling and recharge-zone chemistry \parencite{Tweed2018,Dragon2016}, deep-percolation analysis and aquifer-layer characterisation **[CITATION CHECKED: KAMRA1991]**, greater use of test wells with attention to biofouling \parencite{Stuetz2004}, transient tests of steady-state assumptions \parencite{Schilling2022}, and unsteady flow and mass-transport models with stochastic analysis at watershed scale \parencite{Gates2002,Burkhalter2006}. Contemporary needs also span unsaturated and preferential-flow modules for disconnected groundwater \parencite{Kompanizare2024}, independent methods for layer-to-layer drainage under preferential flow \parencite{Ojeda2018}, dynamic frozen-soil and air-temperature models with measured soil structure and P \parencite{Ulén2016}, and machine-learning surrogates trained across diverse climatic and hydrogeological conditions with transient processes and real-time control \parencite{Lei2026}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Practice-scale treatment: wetlands, buffers, bioreactors, and recycling
claim_paragraph: Detailed process modelling of individual conservation practices is a recurring need. Hourly-time-step dynamic modelling is required to approximate nitrate removal in tile-fed wetlands, with means to buffer and gradually release flows \parencite{Tanner2011}; constructed-wetland siting and sizing depend on wetland-to-catchment ratio and seasonal discharge, requiring long-term study of sustainable nitrogen-retention efficiency, N\textsubscript{2}O emission processes, and pesticide-metabolite accumulation \parencite{Steidl2019,Tournebize2017,Kovacic2006,Haverstock2017}. Passing tile-drained water through wetlands is a leading nitrogen-load strategy motivating basin-scale siting analyses \parencite{Baeumler2020,Billy2013,Madramootoo2007,Kadlec2012}. Edge-of-field systems present gaps in surface/subsurface nitrogen removal and phosphorus-plant harvest \parencite{Gordon2021}, verification of design retention times and hydraulic conductivity in bioreactors \parencite{Feyereisen2015}, and placement of drainage beneath vegetative filter strips \parencite{Bhattarai2009}; phosphorus-sorbing filters need testing at higher loadings in both pathways, and filter and grass strips need dormant-season and harvest evaluation \parencite{Plach2023,Holly2016,Vallée2015}. For drainage water recycling, long-term moisture-sensor and automated monitoring, DRAINMOD-DWR-aided design, and economic optimisation are sought **[CITATION CHECKED: Kaur2021]**, alongside regional economic-benefit and reservoir-sizing analyses under future climate \parencite{Kosari2024,Li2021b}. Whether drainage water management within channelized streams can restore natural hydrology, and how it affects headwater biogeochemistry, requires integrated hydrology--water-quality--ecology assessment \parencite{King2009,Sunohara2015,Dalzell2018}, and multipurpose oxbows and restored floodplains warrant continued monitoring \parencite{Leberg2024,Schilling2017,ElAgha2020,AbdelDayem2007}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Preferential and macropore flow: characterisation and modelling
claim_paragraph: The representation of preferential flow is perhaps the most frequently cited frontier, and the recurring theme is that its contribution to drains must be characterised as a function of soil type, water content, and agricultural practice before models can be extrapolated. \textcite{Gaillot2023} and \textcite{Fox2004} call for more mechanistic characterisation of macropore--drain connectivity and of the ``express fraction'' under varying saturated--unsaturated conditions above the drain, with testing across climate, soil, drain configuration, and chemical application. \textcite{Askar2020} stress that rigorous testing of DRAINMOD's empirical macropore approach requires water-table-depth measurements alongside drainage and runoff, direct macropore-flow inputs, and detailed crack geometry and temporal crack dynamics. Process improvements are proposed across frameworks: better matrix--macropore water partitioning and calibration against sub-hourly drainage in RZWQM2 **[CITATION CHECKED: Li2023d]**; dynamic macropore connectivity or effective macroporosity and a soil-moisture transfer factor at watershed scale \parencite{Poon2021}; micropore diffusion and additional domains, with site-specific matrix and macropore conductivity, in dual-permeability descriptions \parencite{Villholth1998,Villholth1998b}; and hysteresis and biopore-flow initiation validated across the profile \parencite{Holbak2021}. Structural controls that models neglect include manure-driven macropore development \parencite{Zhao2001}, crack re-establishment and nutrient transfer in EPIC \parencite{Wang2022}, and calibrated macropore conductivity within a three-dimensional dual-permeability model \parencite{Varvaris2018}. Direct identification of pathways is repeatedly urged---ground-penetrating radar and tracers with explicit flowpath and open-ditch representation \parencite{Tähtikarhu2025}, tracer-tracked routes with solute-transport simulation \parencite{Salo2017}, dye-staining of pathways reaching tile lines \parencite{Nielsen2015}, and characterisation of near-surface pathways across settings \parencite{Frey2012,Allaire2011}. Central quantitative questions remain the fraction of phosphorus and other solutes delivered via preferential versus matrix flow \parencite{King2015,Williams2016}, the range of macropore flows to drains across soils and management \parencite{Reid2012}, whether vertical macropore transport occurs in deep saturated layers \parencite{Villholth1998}, and by-pass flow through cracks for full-year model application \parencite{LESAFFRE1988,BACKLUND1995,Ruark2009}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Long-term, year-round, and multi-scale monitoring
claim_paragraph: Across nutrient, salt, and hydrological studies, authors emphasise that short, seasonally incomplete records mislead. Year-round measurement of flow and concentration, for at least several years on new sites, is deemed necessary to set management priorities and to partition tile flow from surface runoff at watershed scale \parencite{Kladivko2001}. \textcite{Sharpley2019} present a broad agenda: closing water and nutrient balances, studying legacy N and P pools, quantifying snowmelt-driven losses, and evaluating single, stacked, and edge-of-field practices. \textcite{Frankenberger2024} detail monitoring recommendations for drainage water management---high-frequency discharge, runoff, and seepage to close the water budget; process measurements of microbial activity, denitrification, soil-P pools, and redox; consistent documentation of design and management; and a publicly available dataset. Long-term records are singled out as necessary to disentangle land-management from climate-change effects, with the corollary that policy evaluation demands patience \parencite{Bauwe2020,Kelley2017,Gillingham2000,Lemke2011}. Long-term monitoring is likewise sought for edge-of-field and treatment systems---biofouling of recycled-concrete-aggregate drains \parencite{McCulloch2017}, maturation of constructed wetlands for P retention **[CITATION CHECKED: Mendes2020]**, stormwater-retention devices \parencite{Xu2022}, and cumulative groundwater-level effects \parencite{Okuda2020}---and for tracking soil physical, biological, and carbon properties over time \parencite{Frankl2023,Furukawa2008}. Tracer and water-age studies add specific demands: high-frequency tracer measurements to quantify water ages and represent both celerities and velocities \parencite{Williams2021}, event sampling and bulk-soil-water isotopes to constrain young-water fractions \parencite{DimitrovaPetrova2020}, high-resolution specific conductance for end-member mixing \parencite{Kronholm2015,Schilling2019}, and water-isotope or conservative-tracer studies to partition quick flow and baseflow \parencite{Frederiksen2023}. National drainage-extent datasets open new analyses but require clarification of how farmers report ambiguous cases \parencite{Jame2022}, and coordinated international collaboration with consistent reporting of basic performance parameters is urged for treatment systems \parencite{Messer2021,Sims1998}.

Subirrigation embedded in regional water systems is a distinct, largely unresolved frontier: regional water needs should be known before responsible incorporation, with optimised pumping and cautious use of alternative resources \parencite{deWit2022}, and SWAP-type modelling can pre-screen sites and forecast consequences before implementation \parencite{deWit2024}. Seepage effects on CD performance need coordinated experimental and modelling research, including guard lines to evaluate lateral seepage \parencite{Youssef2021,Pease2017,Ale2009}, and excess-moisture stress, spring drawdown, and spring nitrogen loading are priorities \parencite{Craft2018,Lahdou2019}. Anticipatory, forecast-based management should incorporate evapotranspiration, subirrigation, and spatially variable seepage and address forecast uncertainty \parencite{VandeCraats2021}, collector-ditch water-level and control schedules should be optimised \parencite{Salla2022,Strock2025b}, and CD should be paired with local crop and climate characteristics without overlooking rapid water-table decrease raising irrigation demand in dry summers \parencite{Güngör2023,Dou2023,Golmohammadi2016,Kim2023,Wang2020c}. Longer-term studies must disentangle whether soil-property changes under drainage--subirrigation arise from the practice or from irrigation-water quality \parencite{Kaur2023}, and complete water and nutrient budgets within and across field boundaries, plus effects on runoff, preferential flow, and recharge, remain to be tracked \parencite{Shedekar2021,Ross2016,King2022}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Economics, institutions, and adoption
claim_paragraph: Institutional and participatory needs are pervasive. Recommendations include shifting from standardised to flexible, location-specific solutions reflecting stakeholder preferences, balancing top-down against bottom-up participatory management across the infrastructure lifecycle, and linking farmers' tacit knowledge with researchers' explicit knowledge **[CITATION CHECKED: Ritzema2016]**. Capacity development, education, and policy change to lower adoption barriers are emphasised \parencite{Ritzema2016,Castellano2019,SHIRMOHAMMADI1995,Kesicka2023b}, along with governance frameworks, inter-agency coordination, dedicated drainage institutions, and time-bound reclamation action plans \parencite{Singh2019c,Qureshi2008,Gopalakrishnan2007,Ritzema2008b,Valipour2014,Quinn2009}, and awareness, subsidy, micro-finance, and participatory operation-and-maintenance programs \parencite{Satyanarayana2007,Manjunatha2004,BenAissa2013,MCFARLANE1992}. Continued technical and financial support is deemed essential, and research in irrigated agriculture is described as ``not yet over'' \parencite{Qureshi2008,Ritzema2007,TeKrony2004}. Implementation, maintenance, and scaling round out the agenda---large-scale propagation in command areas \parencite{Karegoudar2019}, sludge removal and careful maintenance of aging systems \parencite{Yan2013b,AbdElMageed2009,Lamsodis2011}, efficient site operations and conversion to piped delivery \parencite{Kanber2019}, environmental monitoring and decision-support built bottom-up from project onset \parencite{Quinn2009,Gopalakrishnan2007}, and site-specific selection of profitable, feasible alternatives for problem soils \parencite{MOSTAGHIMI1989,Sharma1998,Muirhead1996,Guedessou2021,Imran2021,DarziNaftchali2017,HARRIS1993,CAMP1982}. Refining the biophysical targets of control---water-table depth by crop, soil, and season, root-development and drought responses, and waterlogging-tolerance germplasm and management packages---remains an active crop and agronomic frontier \parencite{Christen2001b,Nash2015b,Chen2021,Manik2019,Qureshi2008,Sarwar2001,Ritzema2008b,Khorramian2022,Gul2013,Steppuhn2017}. Collectively these directions point toward an integrated research agenda in which improved process representation, denser and longer-term data, and explicit economic and institutional context advance together.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Coupled hydraulics, seepage, and soil heterogeneity
claim_paragraph: Closing the water balance---particularly seepage and groundwater exchange--- remains a persistent gap. Lateral seepage should be allowed to vary during simulation and included among inputs \parencite{Feng2018}, groundwater contributions could enter through double-storage or residual-storage models given hydrochemical data \parencite{DaneshYazdi2016}, and providing groundwater-table data in objective functions would sharpen inverse recovery of soil properties **[CITATION CHECKED: Sedaghatdoost2018]**. Improved calibration strategy is widely urged---parameter-estimation software and multiple conceptual models \parencite{Boico2022}, pilot-point distributed conductivity fields with soil-moisture observations and proxy machine-learning predictions \parencite{Schneider2022}, alternative objective functions such as Kling--Gupta efficiency \parencite{Brighenti2023}, and combined catchment--drainage-discharge calibration \parencite{DeSchepper2017}. Regional groundwater assessments call for radiocarbon sampling and recharge-zone chemistry \parencite{Tweed2018,Dragon2016}, deep-percolation analysis and aquifer-layer characterisation \parencite{BOOKMAN1959,KAMRA1991,KAMRA1994}, greater use of test wells with attention to biofouling \parencite{Stuetz2004}, transient tests of steady-state assumptions \parencite{Schilling2022}, and unsteady flow and mass-transport models with stochastic analysis at watershed scale \parencite{Gates2002,Burkhalter2006}. Contemporary needs also span unsaturated and preferential-flow modules for disconnected groundwater \parencite{Kompanizare2024}, independent methods for layer-to-layer drainage under preferential flow \parencite{Ojeda2018}, dynamic frozen-soil and air-temperature models with measured soil structure and P \parencite{Ulén2016}, and machine-learning surrogates trained across diverse climatic and hydrogeological conditions with transient processes and real-time control \parencite{Lei2026}.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Salt leaching, drainage-water reuse, and disposal
claim_paragraph: Subsurface drainage is a cornerstone for reclaiming salt-affected land, yet its salt-leaching outcomes are only partially understood and only partially detectable with current programs. The recurring message is temporal: meaningful salt reduction often accrues slowly, so short windows underestimate long-term benefits, and only extended drainage with sustained monitoring resolves the true trajectory \parencite{Almen2021,Daigh2025}. Long-term effects of combined saline-water irrigation and subsurface drainage on salinity and yield require further evaluation \parencite{Feng2017,Feng2021}, desalination rates and trends remain incompletely quantified \parencite{Guo2024b,Yao2024}, and controlled drainage introduces unresolved temporal trade-offs for salt accumulation \parencite{Jouni2018,Lu2019,Islam2025,Heng2021}. Better measurement of what leaves through the drains is essential: greater attention to surface-water monitoring of salt and fertiliser export \parencite{Mastrocicco2013}, continuous flow meters and electrical-conductivity probes for oasis-scale balances with evaluation of impacts on downstream phreatic groundwater \parencite{Askri2022}, nutrient balances of recipient waters \parencite{Turtola1995}, and cluster wells and deep sampling to track salinity over time **[CITATION CHECKED: Singh2020d]**.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Validating and extending process-based drainage models
claim_paragraph: Extensions of DRAINMOD are singled out for continued development. \textcite{Askar2021b} call for testing newly incorporated macropore-flow, phosphorus-cycle, and sediment components under varying water management, farming practice, and climate, and \textcite{Askar2025} extend this to the phosphorus and soil-erosion components, recommending that key coefficients become user inputs. For drainage water management and recycling, \textcite{Moursi2022} call for testing DRAINMOD-DWR against field data and for routines simulating the fate of nitrogen, phosphorus, and sediment in the storage reservoir, while \textcite{Moursi2023} add that the reservoir's physical, chemical, and biological processes must be investigated to optimise treatment and to identify when reservoirs become nutrient sources; DRAINMOD-DWR is likewise needed to aid recycling-system design under varied weather, soil, and design conditions with economic optimisation \parencite{Moursi2024}. Related model-development needs include a time-variable surface-depression capacity and wastewater/urban modules \parencite{Abduljaleel2023}, evaluation of a DRAINMOD-ANN model across soil textures \parencite{Awad2022}, and complementary $K_s$-measurement relationships and evaluation methods in data-scarce settings \parencite{NabiSichani2012,Salazar2008}. \textcite{Youssef2018} outline the experimental verification required for controlled drainage---side-by-side controlled and free plots with extensive root-zone, shallow-groundwater, and outflow measurements sustained across seasons, plus a separate seepage simulation---and **[CITATION CHECKED: Skaggs2010]** stress that such experiments must be run at field or watershed scale so that seepage is properly represented, while \textcite{Skaggs2006} note that simplified design methods require testing across wider drain depths and surface storages before general acceptance.

section: Drainage Modeling Gaps and Water Management Research Needs
subsection: Validating and extending process-based drainage models
claim_paragraph: Phosphorus and its transport through macropores emerge as the least mature component across water-quality models. \textcite{Radcliffe2015} provide the most comprehensive agenda: nested paired field experiments to improve P models for drained fields, and structural additions across codes---SWAT and ADAPT should route macropore flow directly to drains, APEX needs a macropore component, HSPF and P-indices should simulate P movement to ditches or drains, DRAINMOD should simulate P losses to drains and sediment-attached P in runoff, PLEASE needs a runoff component, and HYDRUS could parameterise simpler models---with every study quantifying predicted-P accuracy and uncertainty. Consistent with this, \textcite{Guo2020b} recommend physically based tile-drainage subroutines, macropore nutrient pathways, particulate-P losses through tiles, and soil-test-P effects in the APEX/NTT interface; \textcite{Ford2017} seek testing under varied fertiliser management and better understanding of how macropore flow and P respond to tillage, cover crops, and drainage water management; and \textcite{BinShokrana2023b} identify improved fertiliser-P partitioning, macropore-flow simulation, and P-only performance statistics for a DRAINMOD P component, with \textcite{Gowda2012} anticipating a DRAINMOD phosphorus module. Within SWAT, APEX, and RZWQM2, **[CITATION CHECKED: Williams2016]** argue that incorporating identified flow pathways is critical for P estimates, \textcite{Qi2018} recommend a soil-matrix-potential Richards equation and revisiting the particulate-P loss algorithm, and \textcite{Moriasi2012} call for comparing dynamic and constant surface-depression storage. Supporting empirical work is required: further testing of CaCl$_2$-P as a dissolved-reactive-phosphorus estimator across soils and rainfall regimes \parencite{McDowell2001b}, field research on how drainage parameters affect P losses with improved regression models \parencite{Morrison2013}, tests using actual drainage effluent under fluctuating flow \parencite{Sanford2016}, and long-term monitoring of P sources and transport \parencite{Jia2012}. Nitrogen-cycle needs include surface-residue and mobile/immobile-water phases for nitrate transport \parencite{Malone2017}, more empirical data on soil-water/soil-N interactions and complete N budgets in calibration \parencite{Gillette2018}, and deterministic land-use and temporal decay-coefficient representations \parencite{Rudra2005}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Salinity, acid sulfate, reclamation, and irrigation-return management
claim_paragraph: In arid, saline, and irrigated settings, distinct research and management needs emerge. \textcite{Sharma2004} suggest sequential reuse across cereals, grasses, forest plantations, and halophytes and innovative evaporation-pond designs, while gypsum, elemental sulphur, and lime amendments are recommended for long-term management of problem soils \parencite{MANN1982,He2015}. Tolerant rootstocks, halophyte germplasm, and transgenic crops \parencite{Cuevas2019}, land-treatment/pond combinations with restricted hydraulic loading \parencite{Christen2010}, pre-treatment and preferential-flow control before wastewater application \parencite{Duan2015}, and biochar selected for low contaminant content with urgent long-term impact assessment \parencite{Tian2023b} are all advanced, alongside optimum rates of organic soil conditioners to minimise adverse water-quality impacts \parencite{Zhang2015}. Modelling and management priorities include long-term geohydrological and crop data to validate simulations across irrigation/drainage systems \parencite{Yao2017}, systematic evaluation of alternative field-scale irrigation and drainage strategies under ambiguity with a statistical likelihood of achieving goals \parencite{Alzraiee2013}, land-use planning steering irrigation toward low-salinity aquifers \parencite{Bethune2008}, salt-tolerant crops in reclamation rotations \parencite{Qadir2001}, and quantification of rainfall and irrigation-efficiency gains relative to salt-removal capacity \parencite{Castanheira2010}. Water-productivity and technology questions recur: HYDRUS--EPIC evaluation of saline-water-irrigation sustainability \parencite{Feng2019}, water-table contributions to storage and evapotranspiration \parencite{Jia2017}, scalable data infrastructure, life-cycle cost assessment, and low-temperature crystallisation toward near-zero discharge \parencite{Qin2025}, sensor- and expert-informed scheduling **[CITATION CHECKED: Abdelkrim2021]**, complete economic evaluation of irrigation-technology shifts \parencite{DINAR1989}, and continued monitoring of yield and water-quality change to forecast groundwater suitability \parencite{RADSTAKE1988,Karegoudar2022,Qian2025,ElHassanin2022,Ayars2006}. Sediment- and return-flow reduction from furrow-irrigated fields, improved pond removal, and nitrogen-leaching-limiting irrigation and nutrient management are prioritised \parencite{Bjorneberg2020}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Remote sensing, precision tools, decision support, and data infrastructure
claim_paragraph: Numerous studies frame the frontier in terms of improved indices, tools, and shared data. Development of a phosphorus index for German conditions incorporating subsurface drainage, peat groundwater transport, and stream-network connectivity, possibly combined with an N index \parencite{Buczko2007}, and improvement of nutrient-index schemes to include wetland and riparian-buffer removal capacity and catchment soil wetness \parencite{Pärn2012} are proposed. Regression-based tools for nutrient-credit trading via DWM can be extended to other regions with user-friendly interfaces \parencite{Negm2016}, and modifying the Soil Vulnerability Index to differentiate surface from subsurface artificial drainage and incorporate irrigation and rainfall intensity is advanced **[CITATION CHECKED: Baffaut2020]**. Stress s-curve refinement for aeration effects on yield \parencite{Wang2016}, regionally adjustable yield-loss coefficients \parencite{ROBINSON1992}, calibration and validation across multiple sub-watersheds \parencite{Singh2023}, coupling models with tools such as INVEST to assess ecosystem-service tradeoffs \parencite{McLellan2015}, and focusing conservation assessment on managing potholes that drain to ditches \parencite{Smith2008} round out the modelling-and-data infrastructure agenda. Underlying all of these is the data imperative: better, longer, and more spatially representative datasets---spanning water and solute fluxes, GHG emissions, root and biomass development, and management history---are the foundational requirement for validating models, resolving tradeoffs, and delivering site-specific, climate-resilient guidance \parencite{Ma2025,SKAGGS1994,Deng2011}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: This section frames the research frontier around what remains uncertain or unstudied rather than around settled results. Several recurring lines of inquiry structure the synthesis that follows. First, there is a near-universal call for longer-duration, multi-year, multi-site monitoring to smooth climatic variability and capture the true magnitude and persistence of system responses \parencite{Randall2003,Randall2005,Waring2024,Jeong2018,Cooke2012,Kokulan2019,RANDALL1995}. Second, N management---rate, timing, form, placement, and crediting of residual and mineralisable N---remains the primary but incompletely optimised lever, together with the temporal targeting of losses \parencite{Christianson2015b,Bandura2025,Liu2021,ROSSI1991,Zhao2000}. Third, P transport in subsurface drainage is repeatedly flagged as under-studied relative to its importance, particularly for dissolved, colloidal, and bioavailable fractions and for the metrics used to predict loss \parencite{Hertzberger2019,Yuan2022,deOliveira2022,Sharpley1995,Christianson2016}. Fourth, no single best management practice (BMP) is a ``silver bullet'': bundling in-field, edge-of-field, and water-management practices and targeting them to hydrologically active critical source areas is essential **[CITATION CHECKED: Christianson2014]**. Fifth, process-based models are expected to carry much of the predictive burden, yet substantial algorithmic gaps remain---especially for winter, soil carbon--nitrogen (C--N) cycling, macropore flow, and groundwater coupling \parencite{Du2017,SKAGGS1994,Dietzel2016,Feyereisen2006b}. Finally, cutting across all of these, authors stress that biophysical understanding must be coupled with economics, incentive design, policy reform, remote sensing and decision-support tools, and stakeholder engagement before mitigation can be scaled \parencite{Liu2021,Kvítek2023,David2015,Ferin2023,Khanal2020}. The subsections below organise these open questions and priorities in turn, retaining the specific quantitative targets, methods, and conditions proposed by the source studies.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Phosphorus: metrics, mechanisms, transport, and prediction
claim_paragraph: Fragmented reporting hampers synthesis. **[CITATION CHECKED: Christianson2016]** call for more field-scale studies documenting drainage P losses across cropping, nutrient, soil, and design factors, including multiple P species (DRP, particulate, total), and for further developing the Drain Load database. \textcite{Macrae2019} seek understanding of hydroclimatic drivers of event responses and how tillage or P placement affects concentration relationships, and \textcite{Tanga2025} recommend monitoring both particulate and dissolved forms while selecting site-specific stoplog depths from slope, soil, and climate. \textcite{Zhang2017} add that impacts of modified no-till on DRP need investigation and that new soil-P testing and optimised application timing, rates, and methods are required under no-till. Modelling refinements proposed include adjustable manure-P mineralisation and decomposition parameters and further tillage-effect investigation \parencite{Pan2023}, continued P-loss model improvement and representation of crop stress prior to maturity \parencite{Wang2019}, and applicability testing of in-situ optical turbidimeters for particulate matter in drainage water \parencite{Grant1996}. \textcite{Daigh2015b} note that reactive-P concentrations and yields in bioenergy systems need further evaluation where P losses are high, and \textcite{Spiese2023} call for novel BMPs addressing both nitrate and DRP simultaneously.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Process-based modelling: outstanding algorithmic and evaluation gaps
claim_paragraph: \textcite{Moriasi2013} propose using the Revised SWAT model to determine optimum drain depth and spacing but stress that validation of the Hooghoudt and Kirkham equations is needed before use as a decision-support tool. Validating nitrate-load methodologies against DRAINMOD-NII or RZWQM and in additional watersheds \parencite{Ale2012}, multi-year calibration for free-drainage treatments \parencite{Ng2000}, additional testing across soils, crops, and locations before routine application \parencite{Skaggs1995}, and using process-based models to feed databases for economic and risk analysis \parencite{Malone2007} are all advanced. Broader model-development needs include intense field measurement for validation and long-term climate-change simulation \parencite{Negm2014}, improved prediction of high-load peak events \parencite{Grewal2025}, DRAINMOD--DSSAT coupling to capture factors influencing maize relative yield under subirrigation \parencite{Gunn2018}, greater sensitivity to low flows and macropore-flow algorithms \parencite{Morrison2014}, incorporation of CO$_2$, disease, cultivar, and planting-date effects \parencite{Ndulue2024}, additional crop-genetic-parameter calibration and elevated-CO$_2$ accounting for winter crops \parencite{Li2025}, and improved subsurface-drainage simulation within soybean in APSIM **[CITATION CHECKED: Dietzel2016]**.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Monitoring, tracers, isotopes, and source apportionment
claim_paragraph: Improved measurement and tracing underpin many proposed advances. \textcite{Williams2022} call for higher-frequency (sub-daily to daily) measurements, further work on groundwater dynamics in DRP transport, and more comprehensive source-apportionment methods, and \textcite{Hu2024} recommend quantifying $\delta^{18}$O of nitrification-derived nitrate across environments and coupling water and nitrate oxygen isotopes to quantify evaporative enrichment. Monitoring spatial heterogeneity and temporal variability of nitrate concentrations and isotopic compositions in topsoil, drains, and ditches, using multiple tracers, is deemed essential to characterise soil's contribution to river nitrate \parencite{Briand2017}, and boron-isotope analyses around feedlots and fields are advanced to strengthen contaminant tracing \parencite{Komor1997}. Combining isotopic and pathway-partitioning approaches---explicit reporting of surface-inlet presence and partitioning of water and nutrient loads by pathway via before-after control-impact designs, hydrograph separation, or tracers **[CITATION CHECKED: Flores2021]**, evaluating overland-flow versus tile-flow contributions to edge-of-field losses \parencite{Kokulan2019}, and stable water isotopes to verify groundwater flow paths and identify plant water sources \parencite{Islam2022,YliHalla2022}---is repeatedly urged. The role of groundwater outflow in nutrient loading is flagged as under-quantified: modelling and measurement of its contribution \parencite{Turunen2013}, its inclusion in future N-loss studies with attention to non-mineral fractions \parencite{Jokinen2024}, and accounting for the redox status of underlying groundwater when estimating total-N export \parencite{Barkle2021} are all needed. Finer temporal analyses---interactions between drain flow and concentration variation \parencite{Lagzdins2015}, whether near-term flow-weighted nitrate changes predict long-term load and yield changes \parencite{Danalatos2022}, and detailed storm-hydrograph analysis to test event-scale hypotheses \parencite{Kladivko2004}---complete this methodological frontier.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Process-based modelling: outstanding algorithmic and evaluation gaps
claim_paragraph: \textcite{Moriasi2013} propose using the Revised SWAT model to determine optimum drain depth and spacing but stress that validation of the Hooghoudt and Kirkham equations is needed before use as a decision-support tool. Validating nitrate-load methodologies against DRAINMOD-NII or RZWQM and in additional watersheds \parencite{Ale2012}, multi-year calibration for free-drainage treatments \parencite{Ng2000}, additional testing across soils, crops, and locations before routine application \parencite{Skaggs1995}, and using process-based models to feed databases for economic and risk analysis \parencite{Malone2007} are all advanced. Broader model-development needs include intense field measurement for validation and long-term climate-change simulation \parencite{Negm2014}, improved prediction of high-load peak events **[CITATION CHECKED: Grewal2025]**, DRAINMOD--DSSAT coupling to capture factors influencing maize relative yield under subirrigation \parencite{Gunn2018}, greater sensitivity to low flows and macropore-flow algorithms \parencite{Morrison2014}, incorporation of CO$_2$, disease, cultivar, and planting-date effects \parencite{Ndulue2024}, additional crop-genetic-parameter calibration and elevated-CO$_2$ accounting for winter crops \parencite{Li2025}, and improved subsurface-drainage simulation within soybean in APSIM \parencite{Dietzel2016}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Drainage water management, water-table control, and system design
claim_paragraph: Optimising drainage design for the joint goals of yield and water quality is a persistent problem. \textcite{Kladivko2021} argue that more field studies coupled with modelling are urgently needed to develop site-specific recommendations and optimise design for both yield and water quality, and \textcite{Zhao2016} suggest research into alternative drain spacing balancing production against decreased losses. Field experiments characterising how shallow and controlled drainage affect the complete water balance, including soil-moisture-based flexible control \parencite{Singh2006b,Singh2007b}, low-cost retrofittable water-table-control designs \parencite{Dinnes2002}, and subirrigation extended to diverse regions with in-depth economic assessment **[CITATION CHECKED: Gunn2019]** are all sought. Cold-climate and peatland settings raise specific needs: optimising winter subsurface drainage and water-table management as temperatures warm \parencite{Li2025}, evaluating subsurface irrigation to maintain shallow water tables and mapping cultivated peatlands \parencite{Läpikivi2025}, and cautions that severe frost may irreversibly affect ploughed-soil structure \parencite{STEINHARDT1974}. Drainage \emph{materials and installation} also feature: long-term investigation of knitted-sock envelope clogging \parencite{Ghane2022}, straw and crop-residue drainage materials and integrated excavation-and-burial machinery \parencite{Qi2025b,Lu2018}, DRAINMOD-based evaluation of design impacts on production, salinity, and waterlogging \parencite{Ellafi2021}, countermeasures such as combining drainage with raised-bed planting \parencite{Takeshima2023}, and perforation-characteristic and standardisation studies for drain materials \parencite{Zhang2025b,ASGHAR1995}. Nutrient-trading programmes are identified as needed to increase shallow-drain adoption \parencite{Ghane2021b}, and in paddy and rice systems new water-management options may reshape agronomy and require new infrastructure and precision integration \parencite{DarziNaftchali2014,Jung2024,Hashemi2020}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Soil health, biology, and drainage-induced soil evolution
claim_paragraph: A distinctive line of inquiry treats subsurface drainage as a driver of long-term, potentially chaotic soil evolution. \textcite{Montagne2009} argue that quantifying human-induced soil evolution as a function of time should be a research priority, including drainage's impact on clay-mineral dissolution, and that soil evolution in response to climate change must be explicitly studied and incorporated in global models \parencite{Montagne2010}; significant material losses over a few decades make human-induced perturbation a powerful tool for studying soil-evolution timescales \parencite{Montagne2013}. Whether drainage-induced evolution continues or stabilises over decades, with measurements along drains at different slope positions and network ages, remains open \parencite{Frison2009}, and a long classical experiment continues to test whether soil structure is eventually affected **[CITATION CHECKED: HOOGHOUDT1952]**. Empirical prediction of earthworm activity from tillage, residue cover, and particle size---likely stronger for no-till than conventional systems---is proposed \parencite{Ouellet2008}, and maintaining drainage operation and cultivation is framed as a management imperative for long-term soil health \parencite{Singh2007}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Bundling, sequencing, spatial targeting, and critical source areas
claim_paragraph: A pervasive conclusion is that no single BMP suffices and that combinations must be studied, sequenced, and optimised. \textcite{Sunohara2016} state plainly that no one BMP is a silver bullet, and \textcite{Lenhart2016} argue that multiple BMPs in series are needed, that in-field/edge-of-field combinations show great promise but have been little studied, and that wetlands and water-retention BMPs must be developed for sensitive downstream waters. Attaining water-quality goals will require a combination of practices implemented at a high level in a targeted manner \parencite{Christianson2014}. Combining conservation tillage with cover crops, pairing in-field with edge-of-field conservation, and incorporating legacy effects **[CITATION CHECKED: Makhtoumi2025]**, examining synergistic effects and formalising optimisation studies \parencite{Kreig2019}, and better understanding of practice interaction and the N-removal capacity of various practices with improved mapping of tile-drained land \parencite{McLellan2015} are all advanced. \textcite{Baulch2019} lay out a broad cold-region programme---comparing surface, tile, and undrained fields; studying CD, channel design, and maintenance through wet--dry cycles; assessing tillage and perennial-forage conversion; quantifying retention in reservoirs, wetlands, and buffers; and developing snowmelt-suited tile-drainage mitigation. Wider application of bioreactors, P reactors, CD, and low-impact development, potentially alongside internal-loading management \parencite{Husk2024,Husk2017}, robust cost-effective BMPs to support cover crops and mitigate warming \parencite{Gupta2023}, and intercrops and hydrology-altering management for P-transport reduction \parencite{HernandezRamirez2011,GAYNOR1995b} extend the bundling agenda.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Greenhouse gases, emerging contaminants, and multi-objective tradeoffs
claim_paragraph: Emerging contaminants and biological interactions are also flagged. Better constraint of the mechanism and lifetime of glyphosate in soil and water \parencite{Spiese2023}, investigation of planter modifications to reduce aquatic exposure to neonicotinoid and other seed-applied pesticides \parencite{Schaafsma2019}, understanding of how watershed microbial communities respond to and control nutrient fluxes \parencite{Knorr2023}, and study of water-quality changes during different rainfall-runoff events to identify compound sources \parencite{Fraindová2022} are all advanced. Particulate silicon transport and its coupling to warming, phytolith mineralisation, and diatom dynamics \parencite{Sethna2022}, nutrient stoichiometry and the fate of organic matter in aquatic ecosystems **[CITATION CHECKED: Manninen2018]**, and the release of accumulated compounds and antibiotic-resistant genes in sludge-amended soils \parencite{Ghirardini2019} broaden the constituent scope. Overarching tradeoffs remain unresolved: the tradeoff of increased nitrate losses under some practices \parencite{Derby2024}, the balance between crop-yield gains in tiled areas and downstream water-quality losses \parencite{Addab2022}, and unresolved tradeoffs among N-loss pathways when switching to fertigation \parencite{Gamble2018}. Emission- and load-optimisation is expected to hinge on optimal N rate and timing that minimise yield--environment tradeoffs \parencite{Emmett2022}.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Phosphorus: metrics, mechanisms, transport, and prediction
claim_paragraph: Fragmented reporting hampers synthesis. \textcite{Christianson2016} call for more field-scale studies documenting drainage P losses across cropping, nutrient, soil, and design factors, including multiple P species (DRP, particulate, total), and for further developing the Drain Load database. \textcite{Macrae2019} seek understanding of hydroclimatic drivers of event responses and how tillage or P placement affects concentration relationships, and \textcite{Tanga2025} recommend monitoring both particulate and dissolved forms while selecting site-specific stoplog depths from slope, soil, and climate. \textcite{Zhang2017} add that impacts of modified no-till on DRP need investigation and that new soil-P testing and optimised application timing, rates, and methods are required under no-till. Modelling refinements proposed include adjustable manure-P mineralisation and decomposition parameters and further tillage-effect investigation **[CITATION CHECKED: Pan2023]**, continued P-loss model improvement and representation of crop stress prior to maturity \parencite{Wang2019}, and applicability testing of in-situ optical turbidimeters for particulate matter in drainage water \parencite{Grant1996}. \textcite{Daigh2015b} note that reactive-P concentrations and yields in bioenergy systems need further evaluation where P losses are high, and \textcite{Spiese2023} call for novel BMPs addressing both nitrate and DRP simultaneously.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Climate change, extremes, and system resilience
claim_paragraph: Climate adaptation frames many priorities. \textcite{Saha2024} stress continuing to identify practices and combinations that increase the resilience of agricultural systems to climate extremes across additional soils and longer periods, and \textcite{Malone2020} lay out a modelling agenda addressing additional periods, representation concentration pathways, management options, cultivars, cover-crop types, and soils. Within-county variation in fertiliser rate, crop-specific manure applications, and multiple global-climate-model forcings from CMIP5 or CMIP6, with attention to perennial-grass co-benefits, are advanced \parencite{Ferin2023}, and cropping systems designed to function under both drought and flood---with engineering solutions such as capturing excess floodwater---are prioritised \parencite{Dietzel2016}. Costs and benefits of adaptation to changing precipitation, irrigation-investment payback, and carbon-farming knowledge-sharing **[CITATION CHECKED: PeltonenSainio2021]**, study of extreme-event effects on cover-crop impacts for field-scale adaptation \parencite{Gupta2023b}, and comparison of N-fertiliser consequences under warming with best field-management identification \parencite{Haghnazari2020} extend the climate frontier. Testing and refinement across additional rainfall environments, soils, and rotations---to confirm interactions between subsurface drainage and planting pattern \parencite{Takeshima2023}, validate pipe-burial-depth effects on water productivity \parencite{Liu2025}, and characterise responses across soil and rainfall levels \parencite{Grewal2025,Negm2014,BENOIT1967}---is a recurring extension of this theme.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Cropping systems: cover crops, perennials, rotations, and diversification
claim_paragraph: Cover crops---especially winter rye---attract the largest concentration of open questions. \textcite{Kladivko2014} call directly for further research, development, and technical assistance to overcome practical obstacles to adoption, for additional field experiments on multiple soil types across the Midwest, and for using new data to calibrate and validate RZWQM. \textcite{Birru2023} and \textcite{Zhao2016} stress that existing evidence is drawn from too few, geographically clustered sites and call for extending scope across more species, soils, climates, and management. On the agronomic side, priorities include tools to promote rye growth in colder regions and long-term no-till study \parencite{Waring2020}, strategies to establish rye under temperature, precipitation, and growing-degree-day extremes \parencite{Bawa2023}, evaluation of more cultivars and improved establishment to reduce year-to-year variability and yield impacts \parencite{Kaspar2007}, cultural and plant-breeding research to improve compatibility and cold hardiness \parencite{Dinnes2002,Liu2019}, and investigation of whether observed yield drag reflects poor planter performance through residue \parencite{Dougherty2020}. Kura clover as living mulch with corn requires better agronomic management to avoid yield loss **[CITATION CHECKED: Qi2011b]**.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Nitrogen management: rates, timing, form, crediting, and loss timing
claim_paragraph: A recurring, more specific gap is the crediting of N supplied by soil organic matter, prior legumes, manure, and land-use legacies when setting rates. \textcite{Bakhsh2007,Bakhsh2005} call for assessing proper N credit from mineralisation of the soil organic-matter pool and soybean residue, and the storage of mineralisable N in the root zone, before applications. \textcite{Randall2001} extend this to improved soil-N testing methods to estimate mineralisable and carryover N, especially after dry years, legumes, or manure---echoed by a recommended spring soil-N test following dry years to credit residual nitrate **[CITATION CHECKED: RANDALL1995]** and by measuring mineral N to evaluate leaching potential before sowing \parencite{Conrad2009}. In systems transitioning from perennial cover, \textcite{Huggins2001} propose second-year N credits for mineralisation following grass conversion, and \textcite{ROBBINS1980} counsel care in setting rates and timing on land plowed out of alfalfa. For irrigated vulnerable soils, \textcite{Derby2009} recommend reducing N in early irrigation years, setting reasonable yield goals, crediting fall residual nitrate, and pursuing field-scale studies spanning soil, vadose-zone, and groundwater. The role of \emph{legacy} N is itself flagged as underexplored: a clearer definition of legacy nutrients is urgently needed to apportion losses \parencite{Williams2022}, and the coupled biogeochemical and hydrological processes regulating legacy-N formation and its impact on nitrate export in tile-drained agroecosystems require dedicated study \parencite{Hu2024}. Better quantification of fertiliser rates and timing, and reconsideration of fall application under warmer winters, would sharpen estimates of management influence on nitrate transport \parencite{Gentry2014}, and further quantification of soil N in growing and non-growing seasons is advised \parencite{Bosompemaa2021}. Emerging tooling---resin-membrane strips to characterise soil-N cycling \parencite{Masri2024}---and better predictions of long-term flow-weighted N concentrations for benchmark soils under typical rotations \parencite{Skaggs2012} round out this agenda.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Cropping systems: cover crops, perennials, rotations, and diversification
claim_paragraph: Perennial and land-use-change options feature prominently. Poorly drained depressions are proposed as candidates for perennial bioenergy crops such as \textit{Miscanthus $\times$ giganteus} or wetland restoration \parencite{Huang2023}, and keeping soil covered year-round with a growing crop such as perennial ley is judged the most effective way to mitigate N losses, while the P focus should be on decreasing surface runoff \parencite{Norberg2022}. Additional data on alfalfa's effect on subsurface discharge during large events across diverse geographies are sought \parencite{Arrueta2025}, and a clear causal link between perennial-crop implementation and nutrient loads across soils is called for, alongside policies rewarding environmental services \parencite{Arrueta2022}. Robust observed water-quality datasets for perennialised systems \parencite{Wilson2023}, large-scale assessment of bioenergy-crop scenarios with cost--benefit analysis to alleviate Gulf of Mexico hypoxia \parencite{Guo2018}, and research on the value of and payments for externalities such as P, sediment, greenhouse-gas, and biodiversity benefits of switchgrass \parencite{Woodbury2018} extend this agenda. Rotation and diversification questions recur: constraining crop-rotation impacts on yield-scaled N loss and accounting for losses on a rotation rather than annual basis \parencite{Zhao2016}, the paucity of research on desirable rotation crops in two-crop Midwestern systems \parencite{Pasley2021}, alternative perennial-containing systems and partial conversion of cropland to pasture or wetland to attain nitrate TMDLs **[CITATION CHECKED: Randall2001]**, and explicit evaluation of controlled drainage, rotation, cover crops, and N management together \parencite{Ma2007b}. Novel options such as intercropping triticale with red clover and developing winter triticale \parencite{Nance2007}, camelina--soybean relay- and double-cropping \parencite{Emmett2022}, fertilised/harvested rye for revenue and net energy \parencite{Malone2018,Malone2023}, and a diverse cropping system documented against the conventional two-year rotation \parencite{Gentry2025} are all advanced for study. \textcite{Dinnes2002} call broadly for perennial cash-cropping systems that maintain returns while reducing leaching, and \textcite{Jaynes2001} conclude that dramatic management change on artificially drained soils will be required before corn production can be considered sustainable.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Economics, incentives, policy, adoption, and the human dimension
claim_paragraph: Adoption, capacity, and social dimensions are stressed across contexts. Detailed cost-benefit analyses, joint farmer--researcher experimentation, and capacity building are prioritised, with adoption depending on farmers' long-term cost-benefit perspective \parencite{Okwany2016}; creating know-how and farmer confidence before project execution is emphasised \parencite{Ghumman2011}; and key practice-use issues---where to apply BMPs, tool availability, how to bundle, and transferability to commercial farms---are identified \parencite{Ward2018}. Stakeholder willingness to adopt must inform proposed measures \parencite{Cuevas2019}, and research integrating ecological, pollution-related, and economic impacts of alternative land uses, with models for optimal policy design, is urged \parencite{Saikkonen2014}. In salinity and irrigation contexts, packages spanning reduced rice plantings, farmer compensation, flexible cost-recovery, and gradual subsidy liberalisation \parencite{Kotb2000}, and analysis showing that feasible drainage-water recycling requires markedly higher, less volatile irrigated yields and lower adoption costs \parencite{Sellars2022} are advanced. Economics of cover crops \parencite{Waring2020}, quantification of soil-health and P-loss impacts to guide subsidies **[CITATION CHECKED: Roth2018]**, long-term cumulative yield-and-profit assessment of drainage installation \parencite{Mourtzinis2021}, producer-participation and pilot-programme information for policy optimisation \parencite{Malone2023}, integrated biophysical--economic modelling at field scale \parencite{Ferin2023}, replicable studies in the Lower Mississippi Alluvial Valley for policy analysis \parencite{Kröger2012}, and landscape-zone management with decision tools accounting for soil effects on yield \parencite{Bakhsh2007b,Nelson2011,Kanwar1997} together define the economic and policy dimension.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Nitrogen management: rates, timing, form, crediting, and loss timing
claim_paragraph: A recurring, more specific gap is the crediting of N supplied by soil organic matter, prior legumes, manure, and land-use legacies when setting rates. \textcite{Bakhsh2007,Bakhsh2005} call for assessing proper N credit from mineralisation of the soil organic-matter pool and soybean residue, and the storage of mineralisable N in the root zone, before applications. \textcite{Randall2001} extend this to improved soil-N testing methods to estimate mineralisable and carryover N, especially after dry years, legumes, or manure---echoed by a recommended spring soil-N test following dry years to credit residual nitrate \parencite{RANDALL1995} and by measuring mineral N to evaluate leaching potential before sowing \parencite{Conrad2009}. In systems transitioning from perennial cover, \textcite{Huggins2001} propose second-year N credits for mineralisation following grass conversion, and \textcite{ROBBINS1980} counsel care in setting rates and timing on land plowed out of alfalfa. For irrigated vulnerable soils, \textcite{Derby2009} recommend reducing N in early irrigation years, setting reasonable yield goals, crediting fall residual nitrate, and pursuing field-scale studies spanning soil, vadose-zone, and groundwater. The role of \emph{legacy} N is itself flagged as underexplored: a clearer definition of legacy nutrients is urgently needed to apportion losses \parencite{Williams2022}, and the coupled biogeochemical and hydrological processes regulating legacy-N formation and its impact on nitrate export in tile-drained agroecosystems require dedicated study \parencite{Hu2024}. Better quantification of fertiliser rates and timing, and reconsideration of fall application under warmer winters, would sharpen estimates of management influence on nitrate transport \parencite{Gentry2014}, and further quantification of soil N in growing and non-growing seasons is advised \parencite{Bosompemaa2021}. Emerging tooling---resin-membrane strips to characterise soil-N cycling \parencite{Masri2024}---and better predictions of long-term flow-weighted N concentrations for benchmark soils under typical rotations **[CITATION CHECKED: Skaggs2012]** round out this agenda.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Long-term, multi-scale monitoring and experimental design
claim_paragraph: Several studies extend this call to non-growing-season and multi-year hydrologic coverage. \textcite{VanEsbroeck2016} recommend collecting field data during the non-growing season when estimating P loads and BMP efficacy, and call for data across a wider range of soil textures, management practices, and hydrologic years---including wetter summers---before drawing conclusions on optimum P-application timing. \textcite{vanderSalm2012} argue that data spanning at least a normal, a wet, and a dry year are necessary to understand losses and transport routes, and \textcite{Ulén2007} note that as long a record as possible is needed for trend estimation because water-quality change may lag the P-loss change driven by agricultural measures. Long-term or continued monitoring is repeatedly invoked to evaluate P leaching and nutrient removal of infiltration systems \parencite{Duan2015}, to determine whether enhanced effluent-driven P losses persist \parencite{Monaghan2004}, to confirm bioreactor and saturated-buffer effectiveness across soils, landscapes, and weather years \parencite{Jaynes2019}, and to obtain definitive evidence of suspended-solids and orthophosphate reductions under cover cropping \parencite{SalcedaGonzalez2025}. Long-term designs are also invoked to detect slow or subtle change---in soil organic carbon recovery under rotation shifts \parencite{Kumar2014}, in discharge-induced organic-matter export \parencite{Manninen2023}, and in whether drainage-induced soil evolution continues or stabilises over decades \parencite{Frison2009}. Several teams describe active or planned long-term programmes in rice--wheat and rice--oil rotations \parencite{Qi2025b}, in subsurface pipe and seepage drainage across diverse environments \parencite{Liu2025b,Liu2025c}, and note that four years of data are insufficient to resolve residue-cover effects on pollutant losses and yield **[CITATION CHECKED: Thoma2005]**.

section: Research Gaps and Nutrient Loss Management
subsection: Salinity, acid sulfate, reclamation, and irrigation-return management
claim_paragraph: Drained acid sulfate (AS) and boreal soils raise specialised questions: short-term hydro-meteorological effects on sulfide oxidation, ripening effects on hydraulic properties, and secondary-mineral formation should be incorporated into model applications \parencite{Salo2023}; the role of the N cycle in sulfide oxidation is unknown in boreal cultivated AS soils **[CITATION CHECKED: Virtanen2017]**; the peat-cover thickness required to hinder sulfidic-material oxidation needs detailed study \parencite{YliHalla2022}; and more detailed AS-soil maps, understanding of anthropogenic versus organic acidity, and cessation of drainage of potential AS soils are urged \parencite{Åström2005}.
