For reclaimed saline, waterlogged, and Vertisol systems, priorities include how subsurface drainage integrated with crop and residue management affects soil quality, carbon sequestration, nutrient budgets, and GHG fluxes \parencite{Mukhopadhyay2023,Mukhopadhyay2023b}, long-term effects of controlled drainage on salinity \parencite{ElGhannam2023}, salt-crust formation and dissolved-species transport \parencite{Colombani2016}, leaching effects on additional elements and organic modifiers \parencite{SoltaniGerdefaramarzi2020}, monitoring of elemental toxicities and waterlogging-stage-specific drainage scheduling \parencite{Qian2021}, long-term root-growth resistance and drainable-porosity determination \parencite{Bahçeci2018,Bahceci2008}, additive-effectiveness and land-replacement characterisation \parencite{Isa2023}, and further multi-location, multi-condition testing over longer periods \parencite{Sadhukhan2019}. Retired land over shallow water tables surrounded by irrigated fields raises unresolved ultimate-use questions \parencite{Purkey2001}.

section: Woodchip Bioreactor Denitrification Research
subsection: Contaminant Transport Through Drainage Inlets and Macropores
claim_paragraph: Pesticide transport modelling forms a coherent cluster of gaps. \textcite{Wendell2024} propose implementing algorithms describing particle-mediated colloidal transport, delineating upland areas and floodplains together with pesticide accumulation when surface runoff infiltrates or evaporates, separately accounting for macropore flow when calculating pesticide leaching, and continuous improvements in modelling and observation to reduce uncertainty in pesticide degradation and transport predictions. \textcite{Zehe2001} argue that convection--dispersion or transfer-function process models must be improved to include pesticide transport by mobile particles and that application guidelines should include soil-specific interactions. \textcite{Fox2007b} identify the need for a quasi-two-dimensional procedure to distribute pesticide across the soil profile (rather than the current one-dimensional approach), site-specific calibration of the enrichment-factor parameter, more sophisticated accounting for macropore/subsurface-drain interconnectivity in chemical routing, and user awareness of model limitations. \textcite{Novak2003} call for better field-scale evaluation of metolachlor retention describing slow immobilisation, and for apparent-dissociation-kinetics processes to be incorporated in registration and management models, especially for persistent pesticides. **[CITATION CHECKED: Dousset2004]** argue that field-scale monitoring of herbicide losses in drains is necessary to compare molecule behaviour across soil types over at least two planting periods to reliably assess leaching risk, and \textcite{Leu2004} call for more quantitative functions relating available field characteristics to a field's vulnerability to lose herbicides. Analytical and marker methods also need development: \textcite{MUIR1978} note that persistence of triazine degradation products could be modelled under better-controlled conditions and that methods for determining hydroxy-triazines in water are needed for routine monitoring, while \textcite{Heaven2012} suggest 3,5-dichloro-2-methoxybenzoic acid could serve as a chemical marker of dicamba pollution and stress identifying contaminant sources. Continued monitoring is advised by \textcite{Gordon2005} given widespread linuron use in carrot and potato production. Over-winter conditions are singled out by \textcite{Siimes2006}, who call for detailed study of soil freezing/thawing and snowmelt effects on herbicide fate and note their dataset will test pesticide-fate models in over-winter conditions.

section: Woodchip Bioreactor Denitrification Research
subsection: Phosphorus-Removal Media, Filter Design, and Novel P Dynamics
claim_paragraph: Phosphorus-sorption materials (PSMs) constitute one of the most heavily populated research-gap areas, spanning material selection, longevity, regeneration, and hydraulic integration. General selection criteria are laid out by **[CITATION CHECKED: Li2020]**, who argue that adsorbent choice must account for phosphorus concentration, interfering ions, temperature, flow rate, and sediment loads; prioritise selectivity for phosphorus at neutral pH; withstand seasonally fluctuating temperature, redox condition, flow rate, and sediment load without sacrificing removal efficiency; be testable for reusability and ease of recovery; and be economical for large field-scale application. \textcite{Mendes2022} add that the apparently synergistic retention mechanism and performance of filter media at high flow rates remain unknown, and that recycling and regeneration of spent filter media should be verified and pursued.

section: Longitudinal Data Gaps and Monitoring Imperatives
subsection: Extending the Temporal Record
claim_paragraph: Record length is necessary but not sufficient: several authors highlight gaps in temporal \emph{resolution} and seasonal coverage. \textcite{Klaiber2020} call for additional years of monitoring together with improved, year-round measurement---especially during the non-growing season---to understand seasonal phosphorus exports and reach more robust conclusions. **[CITATION CHECKED: Hodaj2017]** stress avoiding gaps in high-frequency records, advising that future studies check instruments as frequently as possible. \textcite{Wesström2015} add a timing consideration specific to infrastructure interventions, noting that it is more appropriate to monitor nutrient leaching after drain repair.

section: Drainage Model Calibration and Validation
subsection: Field Data and Process Measurements Still Needed
claim_paragraph: Nitrogen dynamics emerge as the least well-constrained component of drainage models. \textcite{David2009} argue that systematic measurements of denitrification are required to test and refine existing models and to supply data for all major simulated nitrogen fluxes; their idealised design is a multi-year, tile-drained corn--soybean study measuring every major N flux alongside a full suite of physical measurements, with a pragmatic fallback of measuring a few key fluxes plus denitrification to benchmark modelled values. A parameterisation grounded primarily in field and laboratory measurements, denitrification foremost among them, is likewise judged necessary to improve nitrogen simulation \parencite{Salazar2009}. Within SWAT specifically, improvements to soil-nitrogen algorithms are called for, together with better parameterisation and constraint through more detailed agronomic data, and the routine evaluation and reporting of soil-N fluxes such as mineralisation and denitrification as standard practice **[CITATION CHECKED: Ikenberry2017]**. Long-term plot-scale studies developing better carbon and nitrogen estimates are proposed to improve parameterisation and to help reconcile the persistent discrepancy between plot- and subbasin-scale results, with cover-crop studies reporting long-term C and N dynamics singled out for validating long-term response simulations \parencite{Singer2011}. Better resolution of the interactions between soil-N processes and nitrogen export is needed to estimate the lag time between best-management-practice implementation and measurable reductions, alongside individual site assessment \parencite{Law2022}. Continued measurement and verification of parameters are also planned for improved subsurface-drainage modelling under heterogeneous soil nitrogen, where uncertainty prediction is flagged for future assessment \parencite{Tao2021}. Together these define an ambitious empirical programme: multi-year, flux-resolved, denitrification-centred campaigns that current datasets almost never provide.

section: Drainage Model Calibration and Validation
subsection: Calibration, Sensitivity Analysis, and Uncertainty
claim_paragraph: Automated and global approaches to calibration and sensitivity analysis are widely advocated as the means to make parameter interrogation systematic rather than ad hoc. Automatic calibration methods are called for to support robust parameter sensitivity analysis, with ensemble Kalman filtering identified as a promising option for parameter identification \parencite{Warsta2014}, and autocalibration is recommended alongside algorithms to accelerate solution of the Richards equation \parencite{Sadhukhan2019b}. Automatic calibration is noted as an increasingly suggested general practice \parencite{Singh2019b}. Global sensitivity analysis is proposed to capture the parameter interactions that local one-at-a-time methods such as LH-OAT cannot resolve \parencite{Timalsina2023}; sensitivity analysis is recommended to understand parameter influence on model performance in depth \parencite{Chelil2022}; and model sensitivity to all parameters is urged to be analysed under several flow conditions \parencite{Kacimov2000}. For revised SWAT, further studies are needed to establish suitable lower and upper bounds of the sensitivity adjustment factor, with additional work underway on winter and growing-season water and nitrogen budgets \parencite{Moriasi2013b}. At catchment scale, spatially distributed streambed conductance is proposed for reach-level calibration, and groundwater--surface-water exchange fluxes are suggested both as additional calibration targets and as a possible proxy for the drainage contribution to streamflow **[CITATION CHECKED: Karan2021]**.

section: Drainage Model Calibration and Validation
subsection: Instrumentation and Measurement-Method Validation
claim_paragraph: Hydraulic-loss measurement in drainage conduits remains conspicuously incomplete, limiting the physical realism of design equations. Further work is needed on head loss in corrugated-pipe junctions and manholes under free-surface flow, with the possibility of discharge-specific head-loss coefficient relationships noted \parencite{Bayat2011}; on friction energy loss, flow velocities, detailed free-surface elevations, and transitional cavity-flow conditions \parencite{Nédélec2008}; on the influence of declining-bend slope on air discharge across several distortion heights \parencite{Gurklys2008}; and on modifying existing formulae to apply an appropriate Manning coefficient for design **[CITATION CHECKED: Kouchakzadeh2011]**. Strain-gauge experiments are identified as necessary to generate input data characterising the non-linear behaviour of single-wall corrugated HDPE pipe \parencite{Gaj2021}.

section: Drainage Model Calibration and Validation
subsection: Broadening the Empirical Basis: Sites, Soils, Scales, and Time
claim_paragraph: Extending validation across the climatic and management envelope is a closely related priority. Models developed under humid conditions are singled out for testing under semi-arid or arid regimes, and for improved simulation of rainfall events following prolonged dry spells **[CITATION CHECKED: Prasher1996]**---a regime in which current formulations are least constrained. Longer monitoring records are repeatedly invoked as the route to firmer conclusions: continued field measurement over ``a much longer period of time'' is needed to evaluate drainage-envelope materials such as rice husk \parencite{Ebrahimian2011}, and more detailed data over longer periods might have altered both system response and apparent model performance \parencite{Negm2017}. Continued field monitoring and modelling are cited as the means to validate reported results \parencite{Grazhdani1996}, and field verification is recommended before analytical tools are used for design or planning \parencite{Hornbuckle2012}. Design geometry adds a further, still-unresolved dimension: authors call for experiments exploring drain spacings wider than 30~m \parencite{Mathew2001} and for regional answers to how much drainage-efficiency loss to expect and which design rainstorm to adopt \parencite{Wiskow2003}. Several authors stress that combinations of measures and models must be adapted and optimised to local field conditions rather than assumed portable \parencite{MULLER1988}, and that field studies remain necessary simply to confirm that simulations hold \parencite{Shipitalo2016,Yousfi2014}. The recurring implication is that portability is a hypothesis to be tested empirically, not a property to be presumed.

section: Drainage Model Calibration and Validation
subsection: Model Structure, Coupling, and Learning Approaches
claim_paragraph: Refinements to the physical and analytical basis of drainage models constitute a rich set of concrete, testable proposals. Numerical models incorporating aquifer homogeneity, anisotropy, and varying bottom slopes are envisioned, with existing analytical solutions serving to verify them \parencite{Lin2025}; conversely, results from simple models are recommended for cross-checking against more general models and vice versa, collating several analytical approaches, running numerical codes such as MODFLOW, and verifying in the field \parencite{Kacimov2000}. Reanalysis using the Laplace rather than the Boussinesq equation, and extension of in-situ validation to slow-response systems, are proposed \parencite{Bouarfa2000}, while comparison of semi-analytical, fully numerical, and extended analytical solutions is reported as ongoing \parencite{Wiskow2003}. Recession-based equations are proposed for extension to spatially varying soil properties by replacing constant hydraulic conductivity and drainable porosity with functions of distance from the drain, with the effect of slope requiring further work \parencite{Cooke2001}. A three-dimensional flow model is suggested as potentially more suitable at a heterogeneous field site, with independent mathematical treatment and more controlled laboratory and field experiments warranted to make similar-media scaling approaches more robust \parencite{Mohanty1997}. Solute mixing is proposed to be represented with distinct mixing-layer depths and partition coefficients for the mixing and outflow stages, the exact nature of the process remaining to be investigated \parencite{Shalit1996}. Additional targeted refinements include reconsidering the assumption of constant deep percolation and the treatment of shallow water tables persisting within 0.3~m of the surface \parencite{Kolars2019}, further study of spacing and depth through experiment and steady-state analytic--numerical simulation \parencite{Saptomo2021}, and concurrent comparison of outflow and water-table recessions observed at a single site **[CITATION CHECKED: VANDELEUR1959]**. Strengthening index-system construction and the evaluation of calculation reliability---supported by more samples and additional indicators such as soil thickness, grain size, composition, density, effective porosity, and permeability---is urged to enable deeper mechanistic development \parencite{Hou2018}, and building a dedicated simulation model to extend experimental findings is likewise planned \parencite{Tao2019b}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Fractions
claim_paragraph: A central finding is that particulate P (PP) is frequently the dominant form in tile drainage, contrary to the earlier presumption that the soil profile filters subsurface water to dissolved-dominated. In Finnish clays PP was the grand-mean $92\%$ of TP in both runoff and drainage \parencite{Uusitalo2001}; at Rothamsted's Broadbalk drains PP averaged $54\%$ of TP and was strongly related to particulate matter \parencite{Lu2003,Lu2004}; and PP dominated catchment losses in Denmark and elsewhere \parencite{Grant1996,Brendel2019,vanderSalm2012}. Dissolved forms nonetheless dominate in snowmelt-driven, grassland, high-STP, and organic-soil systems: tile SRP averaged $60\%$ of TP across Michigan sites \parencite{Clement2017}, and DRP dominated fertilised continuous-grass losses \parencite{Zhang2015b}. Scottish work showed molybdate-reactive P was only $42\%$ of subsurface TP loss, underscoring the need to measure all P forms \parencite{Hooda1999}. Because algal availability, not total mass, governs eutrophication risk, bioavailable-P estimates matter: desorbable PP and DRP were of equal importance to algal-available P in Finnish clays \parencite{Uusitalo2001,Uusitalo2003}, and only $8$--$18\%$ of grassland lysimeter TP was molybdate-reactive **[CITATION CHECKED: Bilotta2008]**.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Subsurface Drainage as the Dominant Nitrogen Pathway
claim_paragraph: Reported magnitudes span a wide but coherent range. Field- and watershed-scale nitrate-N yields commonly reach or exceed $20$--$60$~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ in maize--soybean systems \parencite{Gentry2009,Gentry2014,Dattamudi2020,Tomer2008}, and tile concentrations frequently approach or exceed the $10$~mg~L$^{-1}$ drinking-water limit. In three Iowa drainage districts, tile water averaged about $13$~mg~L$^{-1}$ NO$_3$-N and exceeded the standard $85$--$90\%$ of the time \parencite{Schilling2012b}, and across three catchments the flow-weighted mean was $17.1$~mg~L$^{-1}$ with $74.2\%$ of samples above the MCL \parencite{Ikenberry2014}. New Zealand tile drains exported $14$--$109$~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ TN ($58$--$90\%$ nitrate) \parencite{Tanner2011}; Illinois riverine and tile yields averaged $30$--$32$ and ranged to $57$--$59$~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Gentry2014}; and very high concentrations characterise some European and irrigated systems, with Italian drainage averaging $94$--$216$~mg~NO$_3$~L$^{-1}$ \parencite{ROSSI1991} and Polish water usually exceeding $70$~mg~L$^{-1}$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Dragon2016]**. A key methodological finding is that interannual variability in load greatly exceeds that of concentration: across 29 Iowa watersheds, flow-weighted concentration ($0.6$--$15.5$~mg~L$^{-1}$) served as a more robust indicator of management change than load or yield \parencite{Danalatos2022}. Early Iowa work already characterised nitrate loss as ``highly variable and strongly dependent on the amount of water lost'' \parencite{BAKER1975}, and long-term records document real declines: German drainage N discharge fell from $33$ to $10$~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ between the 1980s and 1990s, driven mainly by reduced N surplus \parencite{Hirt2005b}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Modelling Drainage Flow, Nitrate, and Phosphorus
claim_paragraph: Process models are the principal tools for quantifying drainage flow and nitrate loss and extrapolating short experiments across weather, soils, and management. After site-specific calibration, the DRAINMOD suite, RZWQM/RZWQM2, SWAT/APEX, and cropping-system and biogeochemical models (APSIM, DNDC, \textit{ecosys}, HERMES, HYDRUS) reproduce annual and cumulative drainage and nitrate loss well---frequently within roughly $\pm5$--$20\%$---and capture the direction of management effects even when absolute values are imperfect \parencite{Youssef2018,Negm2014,Singh2020b,Dayyani2010,Ma2001}. A near-universal pattern is that predictive skill improves with temporal aggregation: annual and cumulative values are simulated well, monthly less so, and daily nitrate concentrations often unsatisfactorily \parencite{Liang2018,Ikenberry2017,Marjerison2016,Ojeda2018,Qi2025}. Nitrate is typically predicted less accurately than flow, and crop N uptake, residual soil N, and yield are recurrent weak points \parencite{Ma2007,Ahuja2007}. DRAINMOD-N~II and RZWQM2 both satisfactorily predicted tile nitrate in Iowa, DRAINMOD-N~II slightly better **[CITATION CHECKED: Du2017]**, and DRAINMOD-DSSAT predicted drainage, nitrate, and yield very well \parencite{Negm2014,Negm2017,Singh2022c}. Extensions to phosphorus are advancing but remain limited: RZWQM2-P was the first to accurately simulate daily DRP and reproduced pathway partitioning \parencite{Sadhukhan2019,Grewal2025,BinShokrana2023b}, DRAINMOD-P satisfactorily predicted discharge and TP but poorly predicted DRP \parencite{Askar2021,Askar2025}, and few standard models yet represent tile P \parencite{Radcliffe2015,Wang2020b}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Preferential Flow, Macroporosity, and Drainage-Induced Structure
claim_paragraph: Rapid delivery of water and surface-applied solutes to drains is governed by a small volume of continuous macropores rather than uniform matrix flow. In a Finnish clay, at $10$~cm above the tile movement occurred exclusively through earthworm burrows ($106$ dyed burrows~m$^{-2}$), and the base of the plough layer acted as a hydraulic barrier; infiltration above the tile lines was about twice that between them and correlated with \textit{Lumbricus terrestris} numbers \parencite{Shipitalo2004}. Worm burrows were the only structures present at tile depth in a Swiss loam \parencite{Stamm2002}, and roughly $50$ continuous burrows~m$^{-2}$ reached from surface to $90$~cm at a German site, their abundance the most important precondition for preferential flow of isoproturon \parencite{Zehe2001}. Smoke-injection and dye studies directly confirmed continuous surface-to-drain pathways clustered within a $\sim$1-m band over the drain, their number increasing as the water table dropped \parencite{Nielsen2015,Petersen2012}. The hydraulically active pore volume is tiny: field analysis indicated an active macroporosity of only $\sim0.17\%$ of soil volume, yet this fraction produced abrupt drainage concentration increases by factors of $20$--$400$ within hours \parencite{Villholth1998}, and macropore area fractions peaked below $0.009$, correlating strongly with saturated conductivity **[CITATION CHECKED: Frey2011]**.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Herbicides and Pesticides in Drainage
claim_paragraph: The mechanism reconciling near-immediate arrival with small overall losses is preferential (macropore) flow. Tracer breakthrough curves were typical of preferential flow, with herbicides arriving after less than $1$~cm of net drainage, interpreted as transport through only $\sim3\%$ of pore volume \parencite{Fortin2002,Dousset2004}. Soil structure, rather than sorption or degradation, dominated between-soil differences, with greater metolachlor losses in a clayey Vertic Cambisol than a loamy Luvisol \parencite{Novak2001,Novak2003}. Although mass losses are small, transient concentrations can exceed thresholds: Ontario maxima reached $287$~$\mu$g~L$^{-1}$ (atrazine) in tile discharge, with the atrazine MCL exceeded in $60\%$ of tile samples \parencite{GAYNOR1995}, and Iowa subsurface drains had glyphosate maxima above $250$~$\mu$g~L$^{-1}$ \parencite{Coupe2012}. Degradates contribute meaningfully and can be more mobile than parents: deethylatrazine accounted for $10$--$27\%$ of combined loss **[CITATION CHECKED: JAYACHANDRAN1994]**. Management levers include banding, residue-conserving tillage with intercrops (reducing loss $46$--$49\%$), and application-timing restriction via a soil-wetness index \parencite{Gaynor2001,Julien2023,Moorman1999}, whereas corn-stover harvest can worsen drainage quality \parencite{Shipitalo2016}. Woodchip and biochar-amended bioreactors removed atrazine (up to $93\%$) mainly abiotically without inhibiting denitrification \parencite{Hassanpour2019,Ilhan2011}, and a substantial modelling literature (PESTDRAIN, HYDRUS-2D, RZWQM, SWAT+) reproduces drainage pesticide dynamics when macroporosity and sorption kinetics are represented \parencite{Branger2009,Boivin2006,Shipitalo2016,Wendell2024,Novak2003}. One explicit methodological gap remains: no reports quantify how flux-averaged drainage concentrations differ from concentrations between drains, so evidence-based conclusions on that comparison cannot be drawn \parencite{Jacobsen2007}. Tile drainage also transports emerging contaminants---PPCPs, hormones, PBDEs, perfluoroalkyl acids, and neonicotinoids---whose behaviour mirrors the timing and preferential-flow patterns above, generally at low, transient concentrations \parencite{Gottschall2012,Gottschall2013,Gottschall2017,Ghirardini2019,Schaafsma2019}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Edge-of-Field and Beyond-the-Field Practices
claim_paragraph: Constructed wetlands treating drainage are extensively documented nitrate sinks, with denitrification dominant. Across French watersheds, nitrate removal averaged $\sim42\%$, dominated by denitrification ($93\%$), and devoting $\sim1\%$ of contributing area can achieve $50\%$ removal, with hydraulic residence time the priority control \parencite{Tournebize2017}. Iowa wetlands reduced incoming nitrate $49\%$ \parencite{Drake2018}, a Minnesota wetland removed $67\%$ over four years \parencite{Gordon2021}, and Illinois wetlands retained $36$--$37\%$ of N with $\sim450$~ha estimated necessary to cut watershed N loading $46\%$ \parencite{Kovacic2006}. Performance is a strong function of hydraulic loading, residence time, temperature, and inlet concentration, so no single-number design is adequate **[CITATION CHECKED: Kadlec2012]**. Wetlands remove nitrate reliably but perform variably for P, sometimes exporting more TP than received \parencite{Tanner2005,Tanner2011,Messer2021}, with plant harvest an important P route in some systems \parencite{Lenhart2016}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Salinity, Trace Elements, and Reclamation
claim_paragraph: In salt-affected soils, drainage design governs both reclamation and nitrogen dynamics. Sustained subsurface drainage lowered soil salinity from $35$ to $4$~dS~m$^{-1}$ at $15$-m spacing and improved rice yield, with narrower spacing favouring nitrate removal and reduced groundwater loading \parencite{Singh2002,Singh2001c,Gafni2001}, and discontinuing drainage caused nitrite to accumulate as salinity inhibited nitrification \parencite{Singh2007}. Pairing biochar with subsurface drainage improves saline--alkali soils beyond either practice alone, reducing electrical conductivity and raising nutrients, enzyme activity, and bacterial diversity, with drainage a stronger salinity control than biochar **[CITATION CHECKED: Liu2025f]**. Farm manure is an effective saline--sodic amendment producing the best yields \parencite{Qadir2001}, and combined subsurface drainage, no-till, gypsum, and cover crops protected crops from salinisation through soil processes not revealed by soil indices alone \parencite{Daigh2025,Zhang2024d,Zhu2025}. Drainage of acid sulphate soils is a distinct hazard, causing stream pH declines to near or below $4.0$ and elevating Al and metals, with controlled pipe drainage recommended over in-stream liming \parencite{Osterholm2005,Åström2005,Virtanen2017,Salo2023}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Agricultural subsurface (tile) drainage is one of the most consequential anthropogenic modifiers of the field-to-stream pathway for nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), agrochemicals, and microbial contaminants. A large, geographically diverse body of evidence---continuously monitored field plots, drainage-district and watershed outlets, isotopic and gaseous tracer studies, plot lysimeters, soil micromorphology, dye and smoke-injection experiments, and process-based and data-driven models---now supports a well-consolidated picture of what drainage controls and how strongly. Several conclusions recur across settings and methods. First, in artificially drained cropland the subsurface pathway is the dominant hydrologic and nitrogen-loss route: it typically carries the majority of runoff and the great majority of total-N export, with nitrate the overwhelmingly dominant species and its transport tightly coupled to discharge \parencite{Bechmann2014,Raymond2012,Williams2015,Grose2022}. Second, phosphorus, though smaller in mass, moves through both surface and subsurface routes at concentrations well above eutrophication thresholds, and subsurface drainage---long assumed ``clean'' for P---frequently dominates edge-of-field P loads, often as particulate P delivered by preferential flow \parencite{Pease2018,VanEsbroeck2016,Uusitalo2001,Laubel1999}. Third, a small volume of continuous macropores---earthworm burrows, shrinkage cracks, root channels, and installation scars---governs the rapid delivery of water and surface-applied solutes to drains, and sustained drainage measurably reorganises soil structure, aeration, and pedogenesis \parencite{Shipitalo2004,Villholth1998,Montagne2008}. Fourth, losses are governed first by hydrology: annual and event loads scale with drainage flow, so most export occurs during high-flow periods of the non-growing season \parencite{Kladivko2021,Ikenberry2014,King2016}. Fifth, a suite of mitigation strategies---drainage water management, edge-of-field wetlands, bioreactors and buffers, and in-field cover crops and nutrient management---produces quantified, mechanistically coherent reductions, albeit with scale attenuation and N--P trade-offs **[CITATION CHECKED: Skaggs2010]**. Finally, process models reproduce drainage flow and nitrate well after calibration and are established tools for scenario evaluation \parencite{Youssef2018,Negm2014,Moriasi2013}. This section synthesises the magnitudes, mechanisms, and management responses that the literature has established, together with the pesticide, microbial, trace-element, salinity, greenhouse-gas, and ecological dimensions of drainage water quality.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Hydrologic Control of Nitrate Export
claim_paragraph: High-frequency records reveal characteristic concentration--discharge (C--Q) signatures. Annual nitrate export is largely chemostatic---yields rise proportionately with runoff---and persistent chemostasis has been documented in Illinois and Ohio tile drainage **[CITATION CHECKED: Williams2015]**. Storm-event hysteresis is predominantly counterclockwise ($77\%$ of Indiana storms; $>75\%$ of a long-term Ohio record), indicating dominance of distal nitrate sources during delivery \parencite{Speir2021,Liu2022b}. Analysis concluded that intensive subsurface drainage, rather than deep groundwater, was the dominant factor shaping nitrate C--Q relationships \parencite{Liu2022b}. Tile nitrate responds within hours of water inputs: after irrigation it rose sharply within hours then dropped abruptly, with preferential flow intercepted by the drain originating close to and above the tile \parencite{Mohanty1998}, and bypass (macropore) flow carried most leached N in Japan \parencite{Hayashi1999}. Threshold behaviour is common: tile discharge began once soil-moisture deficit exceeded $-17\pm3$~mm and the water table rose above $0.84\pm0.03$~m \parencite{Williams2022}, and antecedent moisture modulated discharge and solute pulses \parencite{Trentman2020,Kennedy2012}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: Drainage Design and Water Management
claim_paragraph: Drainage water recycling (DWR)---capturing and storing drainage for supplemental irrigation---benefits both production and downstream water quality. Yield gains reach $61\%$ for corn and $31\%$ for soybean, with Canadian N-loss reductions of $40$--$70\%$ and P-loss reductions of $12$--$36\%$, and modelled downstream N-delivery reductions of $24$--$37\%$ \parencite{Hay2021}. A North Carolina reservoir reduced TN load $47\%$, TP $30\%$, and sediment $87\%$, with hydraulic retention time the key control, though it was a net source of particulate P \parencite{Moursi2023,Moursi2022}. Multi-location synthesis of 53 site-years showed DWR is more resilient than free drainage, protecting yield during drought and excess precipitation and reducing yield variability $22\%$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Willison2021]**, and adoption economics indicate crop insurance is not a major barrier \parencite{Sellars2022}. In arid systems, integrated on-farm drainage management reused all but $0.7\%$ of applied water \parencite{Ayars2014,Kosari2024}.

section: Agricultural Contaminant Loss via Tile Drainage
subsection: In-Field Management: Cover Crops, Rotation, and Nutrient Management
claim_paragraph: Long-term P inputs raise subsurface P losses, generally in the order continuous grass $>$ rotation $>$ continuous corn, with fertilised grass shifting from a P sink to a source **[CITATION CHECKED: Zhang2015b]**. Swine-manure compost produced much greater DRP, PP, and TP than controls \parencite{Zhang2015}, and about $60\%$ of DRP losses from a no-till cover-crop site followed fall surface fertilisation, highlighting incidental loss \parencite{Macrae2023,Mumbi2025b}. Across the MANAGE database, generally less than $2\%$ of applied P was lost in drainage \parencite{Christianson2016}. Tillage involves trade-offs: no-till and conservation tillage were associated with higher subsurface DRP but tillage increased PP and sediment \parencite{Ni2020,Macrae2023,Koskiaho2002}. In snowmelt regions, zero tillage and perennial forages can \emph{increase} dissolved P despite reducing erosion \parencite{Baulch2019}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Data-Driven, Remote-Sensing, and Geostatistical Methods
claim_paragraph: Data-driven methods frequently match or outperform process models for the specific outputs they are trained on while requiring less data and computation. Artificial neural networks predicted real-time water-table control accurately (minimum RMSE 60.6--73.8~mm), most best networks being small \parencite{Yang2000}, and predicted saturated conductivity more accurately than pedotransfer functions ($R^2$ up to 0.96), with ANN-based designs closer to measured-data designs and trainable on about 50 measurements \parencite{Ellafi2021}. Random forests outperformed multiple linear regression for agronomic prediction (water-table depth $R^2=0.95$ versus 0.28), capturing nonlinear effects and locating an optimal 7~m spacing \parencite{Djiemon2019}. An Attention U-Net surrogate with adaptive weighted loss cut $L_2$ error about 43\% and reached test $R^2$ of 0.997--1 for head, drainage volume and salt discharge while drastically reducing computation \parencite{Lei2026}. For salinity, a back-propagation network predicted drainage-effluent salinity better than SALTMOD, but SALTMOD remained superior for root-zone salt balance, the ANN being a faster ``gray box'' on minimal input \parencite{Sarangi2006}. Clustering and discriminant analysis delineated management zones, identifying elevation and subsurface drainage as significant discriminators of NO$_3$-N leaching zones (86\% accuracy) **[CITATION CHECKED: Bakhsh2005b]**.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Scale Dependence, Homogenization, Travel Times, and Pathways
claim_paragraph: Tracer and geochemical studies partition tile flow into fast preferential and slower matrix components whose balance shifts with season and wetness. In a French field, dry-condition rainwater transferred directly through macropores whereas saturated conditions were dominated by pre-event soil water, with surface and tile drainage transferring 44\% and 20\% of annual effective rainfall and 65\% of infiltrating water not captured by tiles **[CITATION CHECKED: Gaillot2023]**; catchment monitoring identified slow saturated drainage and fast preferential flow, the fast peak contributing about 15\% of water and sediment fluxes \parencite{Grangeon2021}. Ohio master-recession analysis distinguished two reservoirs and apportioned annual tile discharge into 9\% quick-old, 39\% quick-new, 42\% slow-old and 10\% slow-new, showing new water routes through both reservoirs \parencite{Nazari2021}. Preferential flow accounted for a higher fraction in clay than loam and correlated with phosphorus loads \parencite{Pluer2020}, and Swedish modelling attributed autumn events to preferential flow and spring events to matrix flow \parencite{Salazar2011}. Flow and export are highly concentrated: in Ohio, surface runoff occurred $41\pm42$ and tile drainage $240\pm69$~d~yr$^{-1}$, 80\% of tile discharge in 21\% of the year; a 30\% cut in annual tile NO$_3$-N load would require treating tile flow 83\% of the time if targeting low flows but only 3\% if targeting high flows \parencite{Williams2018}. Managed-drainage monitoring reinforced this---287~mm (40.3\% of precipitation) of discharge, 94\% when the valve was open \parencite{Miller2022}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Design Applications and Field Outcomes
claim_paragraph: The validated models have been applied extensively to quantify design trade-offs. Narrower spacing and shallower drains improve water-table control and aeration: SEW30 fell sharply from 3461 to 450~cm~day across configurations as drains were made shallower and closer in Iranian paddies, a 0.65~m depth with 30~m spacing providing desired wet-season control \parencite{DarziNaftchali2013,DarziNaftchally2014}. Design analyses balance aeration against drainage volume, with SEW30 rising and drainage volume falling with wider spacing and mild-to-severe aeration risk at 75~m but not 25~m \parencite{Verma2014,Hirekhan2007}. Optimum spacings for trafficability on Illinois claypan soils were 10--13~m \parencite{MOSTAGHIMI1989}, and in South Africa target water tables of 1.0--1.5~m required 25--40~m spacing in clay versus 55--70~m in clay loam, confirming the closer-spacing-for-lower-$K_{sat}$ rule \parencite{Malota2015}. Shallow drainage cut Iowa subsurface drainage by 8.4\% \parencite{Zhou2013,Mendez2004}. Climate-change simulations consistently project higher future subsurface drainage (about 14--80\% depending on model and precipitation) concentrated in winter, with implications for nitrate loss, while recommended designs still maintained relative yields above 80\% \parencite{Singh2009,Chen2016,Feng2018}. Supporting field studies established the reliability of the measurement and property-estimation methods underpinning this modelling: drain-derived conductivity and drainable porosity agreed with independent methods \parencite{BUCKLAND1986}, Rosetta and RETC reproduced measured conductivity and retention accurately \parencite{Malota2022,Malota2024}, cover crops reduce drainage by a robust $\approx30$~mm \parencite{Meyer2019}, and long-term drainage intensity measurably alters soil physical properties, carbon accumulation and workability, with $\le12$~m spacing protecting subsoil from compaction \parencite{Omonode2025,Mante2022,Mante2018,Frison2009,Roy2020}. Together these results demonstrate that the hydrologic and streamflow signature of tile drainage---accurate monthly and annual water balances, elevated low flows and baseflow, damped intermediate flows, modest large-flood effects, shortened and homogenised travel times, scale-dependent flashiness and peak response, and quantifiable design trade-offs---is both mechanistically explicable and reproducible across observational and modelling lines of evidence **[CITATION CHECKED: Gaj2022]**.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Evaluation Metrics and Measurement Protocols
claim_paragraph: Aggregative indicators and empirical regressions provide a complementary, policy-facing layer. A global compilation of 60 hydraulic-retention-time--nitrate-removal regressions showed strong within-study linearity but wide between-study variability, slope correlating positively with temperature and negatively with inflow N, and yielded generalised median models (NRE $\approx2.9\times$HRT$+0.37$ overall; $3.2\times$HRT$+0.18$ for a tile proxy) \parencite{Christianson2025c}. A soil quality index was unaffected by tillage or drainage but correlated with corn yield ($R=0.62$), $K_{sat}$ the key physical indicator **[CITATION CHECKED: Nakajima2015]**, while phosphorus-loss indicators and the Phosphorus Index are framed as source $\times$ transport aggregations expected to be directionally correct against water-quality data \parencite{Reid2018,Zhang2018}, and a riparian-quality index correlated with an independent measure, width alone correlating most strongly \parencite{Terrado2015}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Watershed- and Regional-Scale Representation
claim_paragraph: Distributed groundwater models, principally MODFLOW, are established tools for regional assessment, salinity-hazard mapping and optimisation. Calibrated models matched observed heads closely (e.g. 92\% correlation) and were used to design interceptor systems, quantify drawdown (average 0.53~m over three years) and predict discharge \parencite{Ghorbani2016,Mirlas2012,Mirlas2009,Mirlas2013,Mirlas2021,AbdElaziz2025}. Sensitivity analyses showed these models relatively insensitive to specific storage ($\pm$15\%) and aquifer conductivity ($\pm$50\%) but responsive to aquitard conductivity, and revealed existing drains sometimes intercepting only 9--30\% of groundwater flow \parencite{Mirlas2012,Mirlas2009,Mirlas2013}. Simulation--optimisation achieved equal or better water-table control with about 20\% less pumping **[CITATION CHECKED: Rana2008]**, a 90$^{\circ}$ alignment to groundwater flow was identified as optimal \parencite{AbdElaziz2025}, and coastal applications quantified sea-level rise raising drain discharge by 12.5--43.4\% \parencite{AbdElaty2019}. New MODFLOW subsurface-drainage (SDR) packages based on the Hooghoudt equation markedly outperform the conventional DRN package, reproducing steady-state and experimental drainage (RRMSE $<$5\%) by calibrating only conductivity, whereas fixed DRN conductance caused large errors and simulated 16.9--55.7 times more drainage than DRN \parencite{Yang2022b,Han2025}; an entrance-resistance modification corrected over-predictions for synthetic-envelope pipes (NRMSE $<$3.18\%; NSE, KGE $>$0.9) \parencite{Qian2025b}. Such frameworks quantified regional salt-discharge increases of 38--54\% and vadose-zone salt reductions exceeding 90\%, a critical drainage-to-irrigation ratio near 10--11\%, and a 1~m appropriate grid resolution \parencite{Yang2022b,Han2025}. Regional nitrate mapping showed high-drainage areas tend to have moderate-to-low groundwater reduction because drainage bypasses reducing zones \parencite{Hojberg2017,Hansen2019}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Field-Scale Water-Management Models
claim_paragraph: Richards-equation codes complement \textsc{DRAINMOD}. HYDRUS (2D/3D) consistently predicts drainage fluxes and water-table depths under contrasting systems (EF 0.91--1; RMSE 0.2--6.4~cm) in Iranian paddies and is recommended for identifying optimal layouts \parencite{Karandish2018,DarziNaftchali2018}. It reproduced Canadian soil-water content (67--76\% of variance) and clarified mechanics, showing that in compacted histosols matric-potential drawdown was 58\% faster below than above a compact layer, so raising that layer's conductivity (by up to $50\times$) rather than narrowing spacing is the effective remedy \parencite{Mante2018,Guedessou2021}; it also simulated higher drainage than the Hooghoudt and Murashima--Ogino equations for paddies and highlighted the control of spacing, depth and cracks \parencite{Ebrahimian2015}. Related variably saturated codes include the CSUID 3D model, which reproduced 1D infiltration, 2D water-table and drainage benchmarks ($R^2=0.96$--0.99) while propagating parameter uncertainty to root-zone salinity and yield \parencite{Alzraiee2013b,Alzraiee2013}, and Richards/Darcy simulations of sheet-pipe systems showing strong textural control of drawdown **[CITATION CHECKED: Saptomo2021]**.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Analytical Solutions for Drain Spacing and Water-Table Dynamics
claim_paragraph: Incorporating evapotranspiration and unsaturated-zone flow generally permits wider, more economical spacing. Analytical ET-aware solutions lower the water table faster and allow spacing increases of about 9--18\% (at $K=3$~m~day$^{-1}$, ET $=8$~mm~day$^{-1}$), applicable even to layered profiles \parencite{NIKAM1992,Singh2010,Upadhyaya2000}. Accounting for bare-soil evaporation widened calculated spacings by 23--74\% depending on texture (e.g. clay from 22.5 to 28~m) \parencite{AbdelFattah2005}. A spacing equation including horizontal unsaturated-zone flow gave up to 30\% wider spacing for coarse soils near an impervious layer, diminishing to $<$5\% when that layer lay 3~m below drain level, and agreed with HYDRUS-2D for non-submerged drains \parencite{Yousfi2014}. Bi-level solutions show the deep drain discharges more than the shallow one and that spacing is only slightly smaller than an equivalent conventional level system \parencite{Verma1998,Upadhyaya2000,Kankarej2023}. For sloping aquifers, water-table profiles become asymmetric with the divide shifting toward the lower drain, and hybrid finite-analytic solutions yield 12--17\% larger spacing than analytical ones **[CITATION CHECKED: Singh2010]**. Dual-depth systems always remove water more effectively than single-depth systems (relative discharge 160--270\%), so retrofitting intermediate drains can raise effectiveness by 50\% or more \parencite{Kirkham1997}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Modification of the Flow Regime
claim_paragraph: Flashiness responds to drainage in a soil- and slope-dependent way. A global meta-analysis of 464 watersheds found overall flashiness (Richards--Baker Index) similar regardless of drainage extent but diverging by setting: in flat watersheds ($<$2\% slope) medium/high drainage raised RBI, whereas in sloping watersheds low extent had the highest RBI, and drainage extent correlated positively with agricultural land use and clay content and negatively with slope \parencite{Zhou2025}. Field-scale Iowa simulations showed drainage decreased flashiness for low-conductivity soils and increased it for high-conductivity soils, homogenising response, with an optimal spacing near 15~m **[CITATION CHECKED: Sloan2016]**; Ohio modelling found overall flashiness decreased with tiles, minimised near 50~m spacing \parencite{Rathore2025}. Across 30 Nordic--Baltic catchments, flashiness related negatively to baseflow index and positively to drained share and intensity, and computing it from hourly rather than daily discharge increased it nearly threefold \parencite{Deelstra2014,Deelstra2014b}. At the regime scale, drainage significantly increased streamflow-drought duration and intensity while reducing frequency, each 10\% increase in tile-drained area lengthening drought duration by 0.03~d, raising intensity 12\%, and lowering frequency 0.10 events~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Adelsperger2024}. Indiana trend analysis found increasing low- and medium-flow trends with weakened precipitation linkage in heavily drained areas, suggesting a drainage influence \parencite{Kumar2009}, while a synthesis of seven Midwestern rivers concluded that inter-annual variability in streamflow, baseflow and N load was controlled primarily by current- and previous-year precipitation \parencite{Baeumler2020}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Field-Scale Water-Management Models
claim_paragraph: Head-to-head comparisons generally find several field models perform comparably. In the Netherlands, WAVE, SWAP and \textsc{DRAINMOD} predicted lateral drainage flux equally reliably, \textsc{DRAINMOD} giving the most accurate discharge \parencite{ElSadek2001}. \textsc{DRAINMOD} and SWACROP predicted midspan water tables and outflow close to measurements without calibration, \textsc{DRAINMOD} slightly better, though both over-predicted outflow after dry spells \parencite{Prasher1996}. SWAP reproduced water-table behaviour and cumulative discharge in India (0.17--0.18~m; 7.8--39.4~mm) and was endorsed as a simple performance tool **[CITATION CHECKED: Verma2014]**. \textsc{WaSim} predicted water-table depth well ($R^2=0.86$) but discharge less confidently ($R^2=0.57$) under Rosetta-estimated conductivity \parencite{Malota2022}, yet was judged a workable design and reclamation tool elsewhere \parencite{Hirekhan2007,Malota2024}. Among distributed models, \textsc{DRAINMOD} tended to over-predict and CATHY to under-predict tile flow, both poor at low flow but good in wet periods, with the layer below the drains most influential \parencite{Muma2017}. For salinity, a saturated--unsaturated ``SD'' approach outperformed \textsc{DRAINMOD-S}, which over-estimated short-term and under-estimated long-term salinity \parencite{Nozari2021}, although \textsc{DRAINMOD-S} itself calibrated satisfactorily in coastal China \parencite{Feng2018}.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: The simulation, design and performance evaluation of agricultural subsurface (tile) drainage rest on several converging lines of evidence: site-scale field validations of water-table depth, drain discharge, salinity and solute fluxes; benchmark comparisons of analytical drain-spacing solutions against experiments, numerical codes and one another; pipe- and conduit-scale hydraulic experiments; watershed- and regional-scale studies of how drainage is conceptualised within distributed models; formal sensitivity, calibration and uncertainty analyses; and a large body of tracer, hydrograph-separation and monitoring work that quantifies how drainage reshapes streamflow. Across this literature a robust set of consolidated findings has emerged. The field-scale water-management model \textsc{DRAINMOD} is by far the most extensively tested and is repeatedly judged a reliable design and evaluation tool for poorly and artificially drained lands \parencite{Singh2019b,Gowda2012}. Model skill is strongly scale-dependent in time: monthly and annual drainage volumes and cumulative water balances are reproduced with high accuracy, whereas daily and sub-daily peak flows, low dry-season discharge and snowmelt events are the persistent weak points \parencite{Gowda2012,Dayyani2009,Morrison2014,Varvaris2018}. Treating drainage as purely saturated flow can over-predict discharge by up to an order of magnitude, so capillary and unsaturated-zone storage cannot be neglected \parencite{Xin2016b}. Saturated hydraulic conductivity and the evapotranspiration algorithm dominate model sensitivity and uncertainty **[CITATION CHECKED: Wang2006]**. Unsteady-state spacing equations yield narrower, and evapotranspiration-aware solutions wider, more economical spacings than classical steady-state theory \parencite{OOSTERBAAN1988,NIKAM1992}. At pipe scale, entrance resistance and effective radius are now quantified for a wide range of perforation and envelope geometries \parencite{Ghane2022,Ghane2022b}. At the catchment scale, tile drainage supplies a major share of streamflow (frequently 40--65\%), raises low flows and baseflow, damps intermediate flows, has modest effect on the largest floods, and homogenises hydrologic response, while how drains are represented can shift the simulated drain contribution to streamflow by a factor of two or more \parencite{King2014,Schilling2008,Sloan2017,BolandBrien2014,Karan2021,Boico2022}. Data-driven, remote-sensing and geostatistical methods now complement process models for prediction, mapping and design. This section synthesises the quantified performance, mechanisms and design implications these studies have established.

section: Drainage System Flow Modeling and Dynamics
subsection: Drain Hydraulics, Sediment, Solute, and Specialised Settings
claim_paragraph: At the pipe scale, network pressurization introduces storage and delayed secondary peaks. In France, pressurization of the collector network during intense rainfall limited and sometimes reversed discharge, temporarily storing recharge as the water table rose and generating a four-stage sequence that increased the lag to the catchment outlet to 10--25~h \parencite{Henine2010}; a coupled groundwater--pipe model reproduced this, with secondary peaks 11--30~h after rainfall and storage of 11--51~m$^3$ (38--46\% of stored recharge) \parencite{Henine2014}. Drain flow is governed by the system parameter $\sigma=K/(f^2L^2)$, maximum flow rising from 0.025 to 0.56~mm~h$^{-1}$ as $\sigma$ increased \parencite{Bouarfa2000}. Combined tile/mole systems modelled with SEEP/W reproduced discharge well ($R^2=0.811$), a tile-only system being least effective (63\% less drain discharge than the best combined system) \parencite{Tuohy2018}, and drain-flow spatial patterns were driven by topography and geology \parencite{Mahmood2023}. Component-scale studies show tile risers and blind inlets altered flow duration without necessarily changing discharge frequency, blind-inlet infiltration declining to an 8--10-year service life **[CITATION CHECKED: Williams2020]**; blind or gravel inlets substantially reduced sediment and phosphorus losses (TSS 14.4 versus 40.4~kg~ha$^{-1}$~event$^{-1}$) with a flow-capacity/sediment-control trade-off among designs \parencite{Feyereisen2015b,Li2017b}. In recycled-concrete media, permissible flow fell up to 73\% at 4\% fines \parencite{McCulloch2017}, sheet-pipe drainage drained about 45\% more water with 55\% lower percolation \parencite{Tamura2021,Arif2021}, and two distribution pipes could raise 10-day cumulative infiltration in saturated buffers by up to 133\% \parencite{Jaynes2019b}. Deep-percolation recharge has long been recognised as part of the drainage water balance \parencite{BOOKMAN1959}.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Reactive media for phosphorus removal: classes and sorption capacity
claim_paragraph: Iron-based materials are the best-performing and most consistently favoured class. In replicated laboratory comparisons of four iron-based filter materials, each removed at least 95\% of the soluble phosphorus originally present at 1, 10, and 100 ppm $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$-P; at 1000 ppm the ranking was iron oxyhydroxide (IOH) $>$ sand--iron mixture (SMI) $>$ zero-valent iron (ZVI) $>$ powdered iron composite (PIC), and IOH held a slight edge for drainage-water treatment \parencite{Allred2014}. Earlier batch work showed at least 94\% phosphate removal for all ZVI and SMI materials, and columns confirmed substantial removal by SMI3 and ZVI1 even at moderate-to-high concentrations and very short exposure times **[CITATION CHECKED: Allred2012]**. Synthetic goethite iron oxyhydroxide (SG-IOH) almost totally removed phosphate ($>$98\%) from spiked drainage in saturated columns, with the original formulation outperforming the regenerated one \parencite{Allred2017}. Among adsorbents compared at identical conditions, iron filings reached the highest capacity of 4.95 mg/g and steel slag 1.68 mg/g, versus only 0.10--0.13 mg/g for three natural minerals at 20\,$^{\circ}$C---an order-of-magnitude advantage for industrial by-products \parencite{Sellner2019b}. In long-term columns, the Fe-based CFH material retained the highest P (99\% of high inlet P, 98\% of low) and was most robust under variable flow and loading, whereas calcined diatomite earth performed moderately but consistently \parencite{Pugliese2023}. Granular iron-oxide media (GNEM) removed soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) below detection far longer than steel by-product media in continuous columns, reaching a final saturated capacity of 1.176 mg P/g \parencite{Hauda2020}. Reviews reinforce this ordering---Fe-based materials generally achieved DRP retention $\geq$95\% in batch and $>$90\% in most column tests, with negligible desorption and strong, stable bonds \parencite{Mendes2022}. Iron-activated alumina (Alcan) achieved up to 94.4\% phosphate removal (maximum capacity 2.608 mg/g) and was proposed as a novel DRP adsorbent for subsurface drainage \parencite{Kumari2025}.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Phosphorus retention mechanisms and governing conditions
claim_paragraph: The two families retain phosphate by mechanistically distinct routes. For Fe-based media, retention is dominated by inner-sphere adsorption forming strong, stable bonds with negligible desorption \parencite{Mendes2022}. Isotherm and thermodynamic analyses support chemical binding: best-fit isotherms were Dubinin--Radushkevich for GBFS and zeolite, Freundlich for silica sand, Frumkin for CS-AC, and Langmuir for both CKD/sand blends, with mean free-energy values indicating ion-exchange/chemical sorption for GBFS and the 10:90\% CKD/sand blend but physical sorption for zeolite, silica sand, and CS-AC; the separation factor satisfied $0 < R_L < 1$ and decreased with rising initial concentration \parencite{Agrawal2011}. The Langmuir model generally fit steel and mineral media better than Freundlich, and all materials showed increasingly negative Gibbs free energy and positive enthalpy with rising temperature, indicating endothermic adsorption \parencite{Sellner2019b}. Alcan followed a Freundlich isotherm ($R^2=0.991$) and pseudo-second-order kinetics ($R^2=0.99$), supporting chemisorption \parencite{Kumari2025}, and for lime-amended pellets the Langmuir--Freundlich model fit best, with saturated capacity rising from 0.69 to 1.98 mg/g as lime increased \parencite{Li2017}. For Ca-based slag, retention proceeds by calcium phosphate precipitation: downstream slag segments were more efficient than upstream because they carried higher $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and pH, and phosphorus was removed in a moving front as $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and pH-buffer capacity are consumed \parencite{Wang2020d}. Consistent with this, lower pH improved DRP sorption for Fe-based media whereas higher/basic pH improved precipitation-based retention for Ca-based media \parencite{Mendes2022}. The pH dependence of Ca systems is sharp in the field: treated-water pH declined over time and dissolved-P removal dropped dramatically once pH fell below 8.5, with 100\% removal sustained only until cumulative loading reached about 500 mg P/kg slag \parencite{Penn2020}. The same buffering principle underlies subsurface CaCO$_3$ precision treatments, which produced an immediate rise in discharge-water pH by targeting hydrologically active macropores and forming a buffering coating near the drains **[CITATION CHECKED: Dalhem2019]**.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Bioreactor design, sizing, and enhancement strategies
claim_paragraph: Several modifications extend or intensify treatment. Pumping can supply additional nitrate-laden water and lengthen the operating season: a retrofitted dual-chamber system pumped at 1.06--2.17 L s$^{-1}$ per chamber, extended operation by three weeks, and raised combined daily removal to 6.58 g N m$^{-3}$ d$^{-1}$ (from 3.62 without pumping), albeit bypassing 41\% of pumped flow untreated \parencite{Hartfiel2023}. At an underloaded Illinois bioreactor, pumping increased treated volume, loading, and removal---removing 2.8 kg N in a 29-d 2022 period (versus 0.69--2.0 kg N unpumped) and 7.2 kg N over 93 d in 2023---at daily rates of 7.5 and 5.2 g N m$^{-3}$ d$^{-1}$ and efficiencies of 57\% and 64\%, with nightly batching giving 100\% instantaneous removal \parencite{DíazGarcía2025}. Electrical stimulation improved denitrification at 500 mA (carbon anode--cathode best) but not at 100 mA, increasing efficiency at the cost of current efficiency and raising removal cost \parencite{Law2018}. Heated tourmaline both reduced clogging and gave the highest removal across tested HRTs \parencite{Ma2021}. Scaling up, a three-bed catchment-scale Minnesota bioreactor treated 55\% of catchment discharge and removed 713 kg nitrate-N (12.5\% of catchment load; 23\% of throughflow load), but sediment clogging during high flow required a sediment-exclusion system **[CITATION CHECKED: Feyereisen2023]**. Beyond tile drainage, spring bioreactors in the Chesapeake region averaged 41\% annual load reduction (up to $>$65\% in summer), with hundreds of springs estimated to remove 322--771 kg d$^{-1}$ at low unit cost \parencite{Easton2019}. Non-biological alternatives include anion-exchange resin, which removed nitrate at both low and high flow with near-identical breakthrough volumes but was hindered by sulfate selectivity and regenerant disposal \parencite{MAGETTE1990}. Reviews add that carbon dosing and woodchip--corncob mixtures can substantially raise performance, though carbon dosing risks unused effluent carbon, bioclogging, or pollution swapping \parencite{Wang2025b}.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Controls on bioreactor performance: hydraulics, temperature, and loading
claim_paragraph: Temperature exerts a strong, consistent effect. In the only controlled Illinois field experiment holding influent nitrate and HRT constant, exponential functions of water temperature and HRT explained 73\% of the variance in load reduction and 43\% in removal rate \parencite{Bell2015}. In South Dakota, average removal was 56\% in March--June versus 81\% in July--August, falling by about 30\% below 12\,$^{\circ}$C \parencite{Thapa2023}; laboratory columns reached 96\% at 21.5\,$^{\circ}$C/24-h HRT versus 29\% at 10\,$^{\circ}$C/12-h HRT \parencite{Soupir2018}; and Michaelis--Menten $V_{max}$ dropped sharply from 22 to 5\,$^{\circ}$C for composted and fresh woodchips \parencite{Kouanda2021}. Cross-study analysis found low temperature ($<$20\,$^{\circ}$C) significantly depressed removal while intermediate and high temperatures did not differ \parencite{Zhang2021b}. Flow dynamics and antecedent conditions further modulate performance: removal was lower during high-flow events and at high inflow nitrate, and samples taken immediately after rainfall showed higher load removal than later samples \parencite{Thapa2023}. In Quebec, influent nitrate correlated with soil moisture ($r=0.64$) and prior-day temperature ($r=0.67$) and negatively with flow rate ($r=-0.53$), while in-bioreactor reduction tracked lagged temperature ($r=0.58$) and influent concentration ($r=0.71$) **[CITATION CHECKED: Husk2017]**. Reaction kinetics underpin these observations: removal follows zero-order kinetics when nitrate is non-limiting (rate constants 1.42--1.80 mg N L$^{-1}$ h$^{-1}$) and shifts to first-order (0.49 h$^{-1}$) once nitrate becomes limiting \parencite{Hua2016}, and can be treated operationally as zero-order when nitrate greatly exceeds $K_m$ \parencite{Kouanda2021}.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Mechanisms, carbon substrates, and microbial ecology
claim_paragraph: Bioreactor microbial communities are variable and shaped by substrate availability, depth, season, moisture, pH, temperature, inlet nitrate, dissolved oxygen, and HRT \parencite{Hartfiel2022}. Culture and molecular work has identified the responsible organisms, especially those active in cold conditions. From Minnesota bioreactors, screening of 206 isolates yielded three confirmed denitrifiers (\textit{Cellulomonas} sp.\ WB94, \textit{Delftia} sp.\ BE1.2, \textit{Microvirgula} sp.\ BE2.4), two of which denitrified aerobically and whose genomes carried denitrification and polysaccharide-degradation genes, marking WB94 and BE2.4 as bioaugmentation candidates \parencite{Anderson2020}. A parallel study enriched cold-active denitrifiers (\textit{Pseudomonas}, \textit{Polaromonas}, \textit{Cellulomonas}) and confirmed \textit{Cellulomonas} sp.\ WB94 reduces nitrate and degrades cellulose **[CITATION CHECKED: Jang2019]**. Nitrate-reducing fungi are also abundant and cold-adapted: densities reached 845{,}000 and 524{,}000 CFU g$^{-1}$ in soil and woodchips at 15\,$^{\circ}$C, 91 of 349 isolates produced gaseous N (frequently $^{29}$N$_2$, suggesting co-denitrification), 89\% showed cellulase activity, and \textit{nirK} and \textit{p450nor} were detected in 38\% and 12\% of strains \parencite{Aldossari2021}. Bioaugmentation shows conditional promise: pre-grown \textit{Pseudomonas} isolates from Danish woodchips increased nitrate removal by 27--37\% at 5\,$^{\circ}$C in a second assay, with \textit{P.\ chlororaphis} PSS4 most effective \parencite{Jeglot2022}, though inoculation alone often fails owing to rapid washout \parencite{Wang2025b}. Community function tends to be robust: under fluctuating water levels, denitrification rates and denitrifier communities were generally resistant to disturbance, and nitrous-oxide production was consistently about ten-fold lower than nitrate removal \parencite{Hathaway2017}. Mineral amendment can steer the community---heated tourmaline reduced biofilm growth yet increased the relative abundance of \textit{nirS}-, \textit{nirK}-, and \textit{nosZ}-encoding denitrifiers, reducing clogging while giving the highest removal rates (52.1, 43.1, 48.0 g NO$_3$-N m$^{-3}$ d$^{-1}$ at 1, 4, 8 h) \parencite{Ma2021}. Biofouling deposits in drainage wells were controlled chiefly by dissolved iron rather than aerobic bacteria or dissolved oxygen \parencite{Stuetz2004}.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Kinetics, longevity, and field-scale phosphorus removal
claim_paragraph: Phosphate uptake by the better media is rapid, permitting short contact times. Contact times of only 10--15 s sufficed for near-complete removal from drainage spiked with 1 ppm phosphate-P \parencite{Allred2017}, and iron-based materials reduced soluble P below detection or removed $\geq$90\% even at high flow and short contact times \parencite{Allred2014}. Limestone adsorbed phosphate very rapidly, reaching 98\% of its 24-h capacity within 10 min, while steel slag, small steel chips, and medium steel chips reached 73\%, 67\%, and 51\% of their 24-h capacities within 6 h \parencite{Sellner2019b}. Lime-free fly-ash pellets reduced solution P by 80\% in 30 s, whereas lime-bearing pellets required 15--28 min **[CITATION CHECKED: Li2017]**. Both granular iron-oxide media and steel-furnace slag removed SRP below detection for up to five hours; after 24 h the slag removed about 50\% while the iron-oxide media still removed below detection, and after continuous operation the slag saturated within seven days whereas the iron-oxide media still removed 20\% SRP after ten days \parencite{Hauda2020}. Removal generally increased with residence and empty-bed contact time (EBCT): in slag columns the difference between 50 s and 17 s was significant but that between 17 s and 7 s was not \parencite{Sanford2016}; longer EBCT improved removal, extended exhaustion time, and raised modelled capacity for Alcan \parencite{Kumari2025}; and P removal rose with retention time in staged slag segments \parencite{Wang2020d}. However, granular iron-oxide capacity was minimally affected by flow rate and by influent SRP typical of subsurface drainage \parencite{Hauda2020}. Adequate hydraulic conductivity underpins field use: all four iron-based materials exceeded the stormwater sand-filter criterion of $1.0\times10^{-3}$ cm/s \parencite{Allred2014}, ZVI and SMI generally exceeded it \parencite{Allred2012}, and silica sand, blast-furnace slag, zeolite, CS-AC, and the CKD/sand blends fell in or near the target range \parencite{Agrawal2011}.

section: Reactive Media Nutrient Removal
subsection: Coupled treatment, co-benefits, and cost-effectiveness
claim_paragraph: Set against other edge-of-field practices, bioreactors are effective for nitrate but comparatively limited in co-benefits. A US Corn Belt review of 119 records found all five practices (controlled drainage, water-quality wetlands, bioreactors, drainage water recycling, saturated buffers) effective at removing nitrate but with differing additional benefits: water-quality wetlands gave the highest nitrate reduction plus phosphorus removal and habitat value, drainage water recycling offered the greatest yield and co-benefit potential, and denitrifying bioreactors removed nitrate effectively but with limited extra benefits and a need for further study of phosphorus, pesticides, and greenhouse gases **[CITATION CHECKED: Mitchell2023]**. Global synthesis places bioreactor flow-season removal at 14--66\%, alongside constructed wetlands ($\sim$39\% average TN removal) and saturated buffers and controlled drainage ($\sim$30--50\% annual N-load reduction), while noting that agricultural drainage's high-nitrate, low-carbon, low-temperature character complicates transfer of municipal treatment approaches \parencite{Wang2025b}. Constructed-wetland and paired-system studies reinforce that design and sizing dominate outcomes: about 40--50\% N removal is generally achievable at area ratios of 1--4\% with minor gains beyond \parencite{Mendes2021}, and paired surface-flow wetland plus woodchip systems acted as nutrient sinks (TN removal 8--51\%, TP 0--80\%), with the woodchip component contributing more removal than the sedimentation basin and requiring smaller footprints than standalone wetlands \parencite{Pugliese2020}. Collectively, this evidence establishes woodchip bioreactors and reactive-media P filters as dependable, cost-effective nutrient-reduction practices whose performance is well predicted by residence time, temperature, flow, pH, and cumulative loading, and whose principal remaining design frontiers concern phosphorus co-treatment, greenhouse gases, and pesticides.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Crop Rotation, Diversification, and Perennial Systems
claim_paragraph: Perennial and prairie systems are the most effective at limiting drainage nitrate. Prairie systems had concentrations $\le$1.4~mg~L$^{-1}$, 2--195 times below row crops \parencite{Daigh2015b}; restored prairie grass reduced losses to near rainfall levels \parencite{HernandezRamirez2011}; and perennial alfalfa and CRP plots had 0.3--4~mg~L$^{-1}$ versus 14--40 for row crops, with four-year Iowa losses of 217, 204, and 202~kg~ha$^{-1}$ for corn systems versus 7 and 4 for alfalfa and CRP \parencite{Randall2001}. Perennial plots had the lowest concentration and loading among treatments \parencite{Waring2024}. However, the benefit can be short-lived on conversion back to row crops: nitrate losses were low only in the first year, then similar to row crops as residual soil nitrate rose, though former-alfalfa treatments averaged 20\% less drain flow \parencite{Huggins2001}. Simulated novel perennials (intermediate wheatgrass, alfalfa) cut tile nitrate loads $\sim$91--92\% in perennial years, and converting all corn--soybean area to alfalfa or wheatgrass reduced watershed losses 78--81\% \parencite{Wilson2023}. Bioenergy perennials also reduce loss: strategically implemented miscanthus cut total N leaching and DIN export 19--26\% under future climate \parencite{Ferin2023}; replacing maize with switchgrass could reduce Chesapeake N loading 18.2--18.9~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Woodbury2018}; and bioenergy crops on marginal land slightly reduced watershed nutrient losses \parencite{Guo2018}. Diversified rotations, cover crops, perennials, wetlands, bioreactors, and drainage control were all recognized as complementary reducers \parencite{Dinnes2002}. Drainage often raised soybean and corn yield modestly (e.g., +6\% soybean, +8\% corn without N) \parencite{Cassman2025}, though on Fargo clay drainage sometimes reduced yield in dry years and corn--soybean consistently outyielded continuous corn **[CITATION CHECKED: Acharya2019b]**; rotation raised corn yield without changing leaching over six years \parencite{Bakhsh2005}, and organic rotations offered water-timing benefits with sometimes comparable yields \parencite{Logsdon2021}.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Nitrogen Application Rate and Residual Soil Nitrate
claim_paragraph: Regional and database syntheses formalize these patterns. Across the United States and Canada, maize yield followed a quadratic response peaking at 9.3~Mg~ha$^{-1}$ near 193~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$, drainage N losses increased exponentially with rate, and yield-scaled N loss rose sharply once N surplus exceeded about 23~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$---identifying zero N surplus as a practical target \parencite{Zhao2016}. In the MANAGE drain-concentration database, N rate was the strongest predictor of annual NO$_3^-$-N concentration in corn site-years ($R^2=0.59$), with the $>224$~kg~ha$^{-1}$ category highest (19.2~mg~L$^{-1}$) and no yield gain above 150--224~kg~ha$^{-1}$ \parencite{Hertzberger2019}. A twelve-state analysis confirmed that higher rates raised yield, load, and concentration, that reducing rate mitigated loss but reduced yield, and that the most cost-effective high-rate scenarios also produced the highest losses \parencite{Liu2021}. A meta-analysis of $\sim$1{,}000 site-years found dissolved N load increased with rate in continuous corn but not corn--soybean **[CITATION CHECKED: Christianson2015b]**, and a 62-study synthesis reported each unit rise in fertilizer-N rate produced 0.12~kg~NO$_3^-$-N~ha$^{-1}$ loss, with rate explaining 27\% of nitrate-loss variability \parencite{Chatterjee2020b}. Historical measurements likewise scaled loads with rate---e.g., 41, 55, 93, and 180~kg~ha$^{-1}$ at 20--448~kg~ha$^{-1}$ applied \parencite{Ritter2015}.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Process Understanding, Models, and Loss-Pathway Tradeoffs
claim_paragraph: Process-based models---RZWQM, DRAINMOD-N~II, DNDC, DSSAT, Daisy, APSIM, SWAT, CoupModel---reproduce tile flow, nitrate loss, and yield with satisfactory-to-excellent skill and are used to extrapolate management scenarios **[CITATION CHECKED: Jeong2018]**. A modified DNDC captured discharge and leaching magnitudes across fertilizer treatments \parencite{Li2006}; Daisy simulated cumulative discharge and nitrate leaching well (NSE 1.00 and 0.87) though daily fluxes and frost/thaw periods were harder \parencite{Motarjemi2021}; DRAINMOD-N~II reproduced monthly losses and quantified that $\sim$20\% rate reduction cut losses 10--17\% \parencite{Ale2012b}; and regression equations explained 76--95\% of variation in yield, drainage, concentration, and loss \parencite{Malone2007}. RZWQM applications identified reduced rate and spring/split timing as effective, with 150~kg~ha$^{-1}$ single spring N favorable \parencite{Azevedo1997,Malone2007b}, and climate-adaptation modeling projected declining yield and rising drainage N loss under warming, with an optimum rate near 120~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ balancing economics and environment \parencite{Wang2016b}.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Nitrogen Timing, Placement, and Enhanced-Efficiency Products
claim_paragraph: Placement and enhanced-efficiency products offer additional but variable benefits. Fertilizer injection and incorporation showed no significant difference from each other in one synthesis \parencite{Liu2021}, while incorporated and injected applications had higher concentrations than surface applications (14.2, 14.1 vs.\ 10.3~mg~L$^{-1}$) in another \parencite{Hertzberger2019}, and injection could increase loss when rate was high \parencite{Jeong2018}. A localized-compaction-and-doming applicator produced 16\% lower flow-weighted concentrations than a spoke injector (16.8 vs.\ 20.1~mg~L$^{-1}$) with similar yield \parencite{Bakhsh2010}. Nitrapyrin generally did not reduce drainage nitrate or improve yield \parencite{Vetsch2019,Pittelkow2017}, though including it with fall N reduced losses 10--18\% in Minnesota rotations \parencite{Randall2003,Randall2005}. Polymer-coated urea increased yield 20\% without drainage but did not consistently outperform non-coated urea for yield **[CITATION CHECKED: Nash2015]**; a polymer-coated (ESN) product in Minnesota gave the most robust protection, lowering combined N$_2$O, NH$_3$, and NO$_3^-$ losses 47--49\% below urea and split treatments while maintaining yield, with the largest benefit in wet periods \parencite{Menegaz2025}. Summer fertigation with reduced manure rates cut flow-weighted concentration 16\% versus fall injection (47.7 vs.\ 56.8~mg~L$^{-1}$) and annual load (47.1 vs.\ 55.5~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$) without reducing silage yield \parencite{Gamble2018}. In Missouri, fall anhydrous ammonia with nitrapyrin matched spring anhydrous ammonia for yield and had similar or lower environmental N losses, making it an environmentally acceptable alternative \parencite{Kaur2024,Kaur2024c}. Watershed-scale DSSAT simulations showed the benefit of switching fall-to-spring N was largest when cumulative winter rainfall exceeded 500~mm \parencite{Banger2018}.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Cover Crop Mechanisms: Soil Nitrate, Biomass, and Weather Dependence
claim_paragraph: Cover-crop effectiveness is strongly biomass- and weather-dependent, and both biomass and N uptake are governed by weather and sowing date. Biomass and N uptake were low under poor conditions, weakening reductions **[CITATION CHECKED: PrezaFontes2021]**; an oat cover crop had limited, inconsistent effects, reducing concentration only in a high-biomass year \parencite{OBrien2022}. Cereal rye biomass varied 1.37--5.94~Mg~ha$^{-1}$ with biomass N of 23.5--45.7~kg~ha$^{-1}$, highest under late termination \parencite{Gentry2025}, and growth improved when seeding shifted from post-harvest drilling to broadcasting into standing crop \parencite{Waring2024}. Winter triticale captured 44--164~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ and reduced profile soil nitrate 33--53~kg~ha$^{-1}$, with 60--100\% of capture by mid-May and minimal residual N below 60~cm \parencite{Nance2007}. Biomass varied widely across sites and years---highest in 1998--1999 then declining in Minnesota \parencite{Strock2004}; much greater at Nebraska's ENREC than SCAL and highest under wetter, warmer conditions \parencite{Birru2023}; low in two of three South Dakota years \parencite{Bawa2023}. Minnesota modeling showed mid-September planting produced far more biomass (7.0~Mg~ha$^{-1}$ by 30 May) than 30 October planting (3.3~Mg~ha$^{-1}$) \parencite{Feyereisen2006b}, and aboveground N-uptake fractions in Iowa simulations ranged 0.78--0.87 \parencite{Malone2018}. The water-quality benefit is contingent on establishment: the South Dakota reduction was attributed to well-established growth in only one of three years \parencite{Bawa2023}, and successful establishment after corn was estimated in only one of four years in southwest Minnesota \parencite{Strock2004}. Regional modeling explained more than 95\% of site-to-site variation in simulated nitrate-loss reduction, with temperature during rye growth, precipitation, N rate, and corn yield the main drivers, rye being more effective in warmer, less wet southern-Midwest locations \parencite{Malone2014b}; however, a synthesized Iowa dataset did not support a strong direct biomass--response relationship, cautioning that biomass alone does not fully predict site outcomes \parencite{MartinezFeria2016}.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Cover Crop Management, Yield, and Harvested-Rye Systems
claim_paragraph: A central, well-supported conclusion is that rye cover cropping generally imposes no consistent cash-crop yield penalty, particularly for soybean. Winter rye did not affect subsequent soybean yield in Minnesota \parencite{Strock2004}, had no effect on soybean yield or grain N uptake in an Iowa tillage comparison (lower corn yield being attributable to no-till, not rye) \parencite{Waring2020}, and corn and soybean yields in rye treatments were not significantly lower than conventional systems in another Iowa study, unlike kura-clover corn \parencite{Qi2011b}. Under projected climate change, average annual crop-yield differences with and without rye were only about 0.1~Mg~ha$^{-1}$ \parencite{Malone2020}, and long-term Nebraska simulations showed no significant corn penalty in continuous corn \parencite{Birru2023}.
