Documented exceptions concentrate in maize, drought years, and silage: in Iowa, rye reduced maize yield 6\% on average over six years, with the largest penalties in 2012 (34\%) and 2013 (22\%) \parencite{MartinezFeria2016}; corn-silage yield was 16\% (2.7~Mg~ha$^{-1}$) lower after rye in the manured Minnesota watershed \parencite{Krueger2013}; and some studies noted modest corn reductions \parencite{Ruffatti2019,Dougherty2020}, while many report no penalty **[CITATION CHECKED: PrezaFontes2021]**.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Several headline findings are well supported. First, drainage nitrate concentration and load increase with N application rate, while yield plateaus near the economic optimum, so that reducing rate toward the agronomic/economic optimum lowers loss with modest yield penalty \parencite{Jaynes2001,Helmers2012b,Zhao2016,Hertzberger2019}. Second, cover crops---especially winter rye---and perennial or diversified rotations are among the most consistent and largest in-field reducers of drainage nitrate, frequently cutting loads by one-third to more than one-half, with measured multi-year concentration reductions on the order of 25--50\% and simulated regional drainage-N reductions near 40--45\% \parencite{Ruffatti2019,OBrien2022,PrezaFontes2021,Daigh2015b,Gentry2025,Kaspar2012,Malone2018,Feyereisen2006b,Malone2014b}. Third, shifting N from fall to spring or split/side-dress timing, and using soil-test-based rate programs, reduces loss but with smaller and less consistent effects than rate or cropping-system changes \parencite{Randall2003,Dinnes2002,Jaynes2004}. Fourth, tillage exerts weak and inconsistent control over nitrate loss relative to precipitation, cropping system, and N rate **[CITATION CHECKED: Randall2001]**. Fifth, hydrology---the amount and seasonal timing of drainage, itself governed by precipitation---is the dominant control on interannual variability, with most annual loss occurring in spring \parencite{Randall2003,Bakhsh2010,RANDALL1995}. Finally, mitigation practices redistribute N among loss pathways (leaching, N$_2$O, NH$_3$), so evaluating them on a common environmental basis is increasingly emphasized \parencite{PrezaFontes2023,Menegaz2025}. The subsections below synthesize this evidence by management lever, giving central place to the cover-crop literature.

section: Cover Crop Nitrate Loss Mitigation
subsection: Quantified Cover-Crop Reductions and Modeling Confidence
claim_paragraph: Synthesizing across studies, simulated and measured drainage N-loss reductions cluster around 40--60\% when rye is well established, with concentration reductions of 25--50\%. Iowa modeling estimated that unfertilized rye killed without harvest reduced drainage N loss 44\%, and harvesting 20 days later without April fertilizer reduced it 56\% \parencite{Malone2018}. A DSSAT application in central Iowa simulated a 57.3\% reduction in cumulative tile nitrate loss under cereal rye \parencite{Chatterjee2025}. Multi-system Midwest modeling reported average annual reductions of 11.7--31.8~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ (treatment-specific 23.9\%, 42.5\%, 40.0\%, 30.0\%), noting these were conservative relative to field observations \parencite{Malone2014b}. Across 40 sites, simulated drainage N loss ranged 20.8--44.4~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ and cover crops reduced loss nearly 45\% \parencite{Malone2023}. Climate-change projections for Iowa are striking: rye reduced average annual drainage N loads from 47.5 to 18.9~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ under baseline climate (60\%) and from 63.6 to 17.0~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ under future climate (73\%), keeping loads below the 28.0~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ target for all six GCMs, the larger future benefit reflecting greater rye growth under higher temperature and CO$_2$ \parencite{Malone2020}. Long-term Mississippi simulation of a wheat cover crop showed nitrate leaching 20\% lower than winter fallow (68.2 vs.\ 84.8~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$), with autumn-to-spring reductions of 19.6, 18.6, and 8.2~kg~N~ha$^{-1}$ in wet, normal, and dry years and benefits accruing mainly in the cover-crop growth window \parencite{Yang2021}. More broadly, modeling estimated a winter cover crop reduced tile nitrate yield 34\% at watershed scale \parencite{David2015}, cut predicted loss 31\% under pre-plant UAN \parencite{Malone2007b}, and combined with a 20\% rate cut and split N reduced load 32\% **[CITATION CHECKED: Singh2023]**; a winter rye cover crop could reduce Chesapeake N loading 11.2~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Woodbury2018}. Under future climate, cover-crop reductions were projected to persist but may not fully keep pace with rising baseline loss \parencite{Gupta2023}, and at watershed scale, cover crops on 35.5\% of cropland cut subbasin nitrate load 15.5\% and raised median N-use efficiency from 0.49 to 1.02 \parencite{Makhtoumi2025}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Hydrologic Outcomes: Outflow Reduction and the Repartitioning of Water
claim_paragraph: A consolidated finding is that controlled and shallow drainage redirect rather than eliminate stored water, most consistently into surface runoff and secondarily into evapotranspiration and seepage. DRAINMOD simulations for Iowa showed that at 4.0~mm~day$^{-1}$ intensity, shallow and controlled drainage each reduced annual subsurface drainage by about 25--27~mm (roughly 15\%), most of which reappeared as surface runoff with little change in evapotranspiration \parencite{Singh2007b}. Belgian, North Carolina, and Canadian studies consistently report CD decreasing subsurface drainage and increasing surface runoff \parencite{ElSadek2002,ElSadek2002b,DEAL1986,Skaggs1995,Golmohammadi2016,Ndulue2024}; at the watershed scale in Ontario this occurred most during March--April snowmelt, with a slight evapotranspiration increase \parencite{Golmohammadi2016}. Polish simulations projected an approximately fivefold increase in surface runoff from drained arable land \parencite{Sojka2020}, and Finnish modeling found all CD methods increased topsoil-layer runoff while raising evapotranspiration and reducing total runoff, with design choices expressed most clearly in runoff pathways \parencite{Isomäki2024}. Increased evapotranspiration under CD---up to a 10\% ET$_\mathrm{act}$ increase for corn---is a recognised secondary sink **[CITATION CHECKED: DEAL1986]**.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Socio-Economic Returns and Investment Viability
claim_paragraph: Investment in subsurface drainage generates substantial, multi-dimensional socio-economic returns---higher yields, cropping intensity, farm and household income, land value, employment, and reduced out-migration \parencite{Gopalakrishnan2007,AbdelDayem2007}. Drainage typically raises average yields by roughly 10--30\% and lifts net farm income where leaching water and sustainable disposal are assured \parencite{AbdelDayem2007,Datta2000,Wichelns2002}. In the Nile Delta, \textcite{Wichelns2002} report annual gross production values rising 500--550 per hectare and net incomes by 375, 200, and 180 per hectare in non-saline, saline, and rehabilitation areas, with yield improvement accruing progressively (50\% in year one to 100\% by year four). In India, the Uttar Pradesh project reclaimed over 175{,}000~ha of sodic land, raising farm income over 150\%, cropping intensity from 49\% to over 200\%, and household income by 53\% \parencite{Gopalakrishnan2007}; Haryana pilots increased cropping intensity and wheat yields by 50\% to over 200\% as fallow land was cultivated and salinity fell from about 50 to 5~dS~m$^{-1}$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Datta2002]**. Long-term drainage also improves the soil resource base, raising organic carbon, hydraulic conductivity, and enzyme activity and improving the soil quality index by 76--136\%, with rice--wheat yields rising 328--665\% and carbon-sequestration co-benefits up to 4.43~Mg~C~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Mukhopadhyay2023,Mukhopadhyay2023b}. In Pakistan a project lowered the water table 40\%, raised cropping intensity from 102\% to 157\%, and lifted living standards 30\% \parencite{Ghumman2011}, and at aggregate scale Indian waterlogging fell over 70\% despite less than 10\% drained area \parencite{Valipour2014}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Crop Yield and Agronomic Outcomes
claim_paragraph: Controlled drainage repeatedly improves irrigation water-use efficiency without sacrificing yield. In Egypt, simple management of existing systems improved WUE by 15--20\% (about 16\% wheat, 23\% maize, 15\% alfalfa, 20\% cotton) with no yield loss \parencite{Wahba2005}; CD cut applied irrigation by 15.6\% (wheat) and 14\% (maize), raised water productivity, and could save roughly 1.33~BCM for El-Beheira \parencite{Mahmoud2021}; modified layouts reduced applied water 30--40\% without harming salinity or yield **[CITATION CHECKED: ELATFY1991]**; and controlled-water-table wheat achieved the highest crop water productivity at 50\% depletion with a 60~cm water table \parencite{ElHassanin2022}. Iranian paddies raised water productivity \parencite{DarziNaftchali2017b,Asgari2021}, Pakistani controlled drainage produced 6.5~t~ha$^{-1}$ wheat with large irrigation savings reservable for drought \parencite{Khan2003,Sarwar2001}, and in China buried pipes raised water productivity, highest at 1.4~m burial \parencite{Liu2025}. In arid systems the yield benefit is often inseparable from salinity control: Nile-Delta drainage cut top-1.5~m salinity from 5.3 to 2.2~dS~m$^{-1}$ \parencite{ELMOWELHI1988}, Kuttanad drainage leached cations and homogenised chemistry within two years \parencite{Mathew2001}, crop-straw drains removed salt more efficiently than plastic pipe during initial reclamation \parencite{Lu2018}, and modeling showed supplemental irrigation $\geq$100~mm~yr$^{-1}$ kept the salt balance favourable \parencite{Li2018,Sarwar2001,Zhang2024c,Yang2022,Liu2025,Guo2025}, though installation without maintenance fails to control shallow water tables \parencite{Malota2016}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Design Levers: Spacing, Depth, Outlet Control, and Enhanced Configurations
claim_paragraph: Shallow, multi-level, and enhanced configurations extend these principles. Shallow drainage reproduces much of the flow- and load-reduction benefit, reducing Iowa subsurface volume by 46--58\% and nitrate by 29--49\% generally without reducing yield \parencite{Helmers2012,Schott2017}; a multi-state analysis found quicker water-table drawdown, reduced yield variability, and 3.4~cm less total flow than deep drains, though with more surface runoff and a lower benefit--cost ratio \parencite{Ghane2021b}. In saline irrigated settings drain depth controls exported salinity: Australian deep drains flowed continuously and exported the largest salt loads (5867~kg~ha$^{-1}$) whereas shallow drains flowed only after irrigation, with low salinity and the greatest salt-load reduction \parencite{Christen2001b}. Multi-level (bilevel) systems cut the time the water table exceeded 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0~m by 84\%, 67\%, and 41\% and produced much lower shallow-drain salinity (4.7 versus 31.7~dS~m$^{-1}$) while removing similar total salt \parencite{Hornbuckle2007}; analytical theory shows adding shallow drains between deep drains raises drainage rate and allows wider deep-drain spacing \parencite{Hornbuckle2012}, and managed deep drains occupy an intermediate position \parencite{Ayars2006b,Christen2001b}. Engineered enhancements alter flow further: a permeable filter increased discharge (about 1.9 times conventional) and accelerated drawdown while reducing runoff \parencite{Tao2016,Tao2017}; combined open-ditch-plus-subsurface designs improved waterlogging removal \parencite{Ren2021,Tao2025}; siphon-type drainage raised flow rates 27--90\% \parencite{Ren2023}; artificial macropore tubes generated flow where none occurred and desalinated the profile \parencite{Chen2021}; and supplementary drainage of a clay field raised mean annual discharge 2.6-fold and cut topsoil runoff by 75\% \parencite{Häggblom2019}. Controlled drainage with subirrigation raised groundwater levels, supplied 170--410~mm of infiltration, and increased Dutch yields by up to 64\% **[CITATION CHECKED: FAUSEY1995]**, while land retirement with drains closed can eliminate drainage entirely \parencite{Purkey2001}.
human_note: The paper is a Great Lakes and Cornbelt water-quality review. It reports nitrate-load reductions and general water-table-management benefits, but it does not support Dutch yield increases, 170-410 mm infiltration, or a 64 percent yield gain. The 64 percent figure refers to nitrate-nitrogen load reduction, not yield.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Salt Leaching and Reclamation of Saline and Waterlogged Soils
claim_paragraph: Closer spacing and greater depth shorten the desalinization period and increase salt removal, though depth benefits saturate and shallow drains lose effectiveness. A DRAINMOD analysis found the desalinization period negatively related to intensity: at 1.2~m depth, salinity fell 55.5\% in two years at 20~m spacing but only 5.9\% in five years at 200~m spacing, and a slightly saline target within a decade required spacing below 30~m \parencite{Chen2025}. The meta-analysis generalises this with climate-specific layouts---spacing $>$30~m and depth $>$1.2~m in humid climates, 10--20~m spacing with depth $>$1.2~m in arid climates with shallow water tables \parencite{Yang2025}. Field and column studies identify optima near 15--20~m \parencite{Wang2020,Wang2025c,Han2023,Chen2022,Yang2022c}, with desalination decaying and sometimes turning negative beyond about 30~m \parencite{Zhu2025b}. Depth effects are pronounced but bounded: pipes shallower than 1.0~m were essentially invalid for discharging salt \parencite{Qian2021b}, and desalination indices correlate positively with depth \parencite{Qian2021b,Tian2023c,Tian2024}, yet SaltMod/SahysMod show diminishing returns beyond about 1.4~m \parencite{Bahçeci2007,Bahçeci2006}. For yield under saline irrigation an intermediate 0.8--1.2~m depth is often preferred, saving 10--15\% irrigation water with little yield penalty **[CITATION CHECKED: Feng2019]**. Envelope and filter design is a first-order control: the envelope factor dominated over pipe material (single spun-bonded geotextile, 3.0\% perforation optimal) \parencite{Li2022}, a double-layer geotextile integrated filtration and drainage best ($>$95\% salt removal) while triple layers clogged \parencite{Wang2024d}, and the O$_{90}$/d$_{90}$ ratio predicts clogging \parencite{Elzoghby2021}. Complex stratigraphy modifies the optimum---pipes should be placed below low-permeability silty interlayers \parencite{Guo2024b,Tian2024}---and deeper, wider drains desalinize the whole profile whereas shallow, close drains act mainly in the top 80~cm \parencite{KAMRA1991}. Economic analyses converge on roughly 20~m spacing at 1.2~m depth as the maximum-return layout \parencite{Chen2025}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Salt Leaching and Reclamation of Saline and Waterlogged Soils
claim_paragraph: Subsurface drainage enables safe agricultural reuse of saline and brackish water where salt balance is maintained by adequate leaching. Blended drainage water up to 9~dS~m$^{-1}$ produced about 90\% wheat yield in India, cyclic use generally outperforming continuous use \parencite{Sharma2004}; five-year data gave relative wheat yields of 95.8, 90.3, 83.7, and 77.8\% at 6, 9, 12, and 18.8~dS~m$^{-1}$ with post-leaching root-zone salinity kept below 4~dS~m$^{-1}$ \parencite{Sharma1998}; and conjunctive-use economics favour blending \parencite{AGNIHOTRI1992}. In China, brackish leaching discharged more salt than imported in favourable treatments \parencite{Li2023}, saline (6~g~L$^{-1}$) irrigation matched freshwater wheat yields with continued salinity decline **[CITATION CHECKED: Gao2023]**, and drainage kept saline irrigation viable up to 6.25~dS~m$^{-1}$ for maize \parencite{Feng2017}, 4.0--4.4~dS~m$^{-1}$ for grain \parencite{Feng2021}, and 8.0~dS~m$^{-1}$ under cut-soiler drainage \parencite{Neha2022}, with cotton optima at 2--4~g~L$^{-1}$ and the preferred depth increasing with salinity \parencite{Li2024,Lu2019}. Reuse nonetheless carries sodicity and accumulation risks: cyclic reuse caused profile salinity fluctuations and sodic surface soils (SARe~$>$~11) \parencite{Mitchell2000,Jayawardane2001}, though modeled reuse over subsurface drains caused only marginal groundwater deterioration \parencite{KARAJEH1994c}. Blending criteria and reduced-evaporation, low-EC combinations are codified as core salinity-control components \parencite{Kotb2000,Cuevas2019}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Landscape Extent, Modeling, and Monitoring
claim_paragraph: The quantitative understanding above rests on a mature, validated toolkit. Physically based models reproduce field water tables and salt dynamics well: DRAINMOD and DRAINMOD-S captured water tables (NSE up to 0.84) and salinity (NSE 0.40--0.92) and derived spacing/depth recommendations \parencite{Chen2025,Tian2023,Tian2023c,Tian2024,Davoodi2019,Li2024}, and modified DRAINMOD explained 63\% of corn-yield variation, with Indiana calibration reaching Nash--Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.70--0.85 for drain flow \parencite{HARDJOAMIDJOJO1982,Ale2009,Wang2006b,DeBoer2006}. HYDRUS variants and their couplings simulated water--salt transport, drainage mass, and crop response accurately **[CITATION CHECKED: Jia2023]**, salt-and-water-balance models (SaltMod, SahysMod, SWMS-2D, SALTIRSOIL\_M) predicted root-zone salinity and effluent salinity closely enough for management \parencite{Bahçeci2006,Bahçeci2007,Yao2017,Qian2021b,Abdelkrim2021}, and analytical solutions matched barrier/mulch and dual-domain observations \parencite{KAMRA1991,KAMRA1994,Zhang2022,Zhang2024,Youngs2000}. A simple Hooghoudt-based method estimated profit-optimising depth and spacing \parencite{Skaggs2006,HOOGHOUDT1952,KARAJEH1994,KARAJEH1994b,Sands2015}, watershed- scale SWAT-Salt linked local tile behaviour to downstream salinity \parencite{Addab2022,Liu2026,ElAgha2020}, and long-validated empirical effluent-quality relationships remain reliable across decades \parencite{JOHNSTON1993,Kelleners2000}. On the monitoring side, electromagnetic-induction and apparent-EC surveys with geostatistical methods enable rapid, nondestructive, depth-resolved assessment \parencite{Narjary2024,Song2023,Yu2025,Singh2020d,Mirlas2003,Gates2002}, and emerging IoT-plus-LSTM digital-twin systems achieved high-accuracy soil-EC and water-content forecasting (test R$^2$ up to 0.97) \parencite{Qin2025}. Collectively, this modeling and monitoring capability is what allows the design and salt-balance principles summarised here to be transferred with confidence to new sites, supporting the overarching conclusion that drainage systems can be deliberately designed and managed---through spacing, depth, and outlet control---to satisfy agricultural production and environmental objectives simultaneously \parencite{Skaggs1995,Breve1998,ElSadek2002b,Strock2011,Ritzema2016,Blann2009,Gramlich2018,FAUSEY1995,SKAGGS1994}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Crop Yield and Agronomic Outcomes
claim_paragraph: Yield response is mediated by spacing and depth and is soil- and rainfall- specific. Narrower spacing generally raised yield and reduced rainfall sensitivity **[CITATION CHECKED: Kladivko2005]**. Modeling for a Portsmouth sandy loam required spacing of 40~m or less (30~m under poor surface drainage) for 80\% relative yield \parencite{HARDJOAMIDJOJO1982}; across four soils, profit-maximising spacings ranged 19--40~m near a drainage intensity of 1.1--1.2~cm~day$^{-1}$ \parencite{Skaggs2006}; Iowa DRAINMOD predicted significant gains with soil-specific optima \parencite{Arora2024}; and Minnesota relative yield rose from 43\% undrained to 99\% at 23~m spacing and 135~cm depth \parencite{Sands2015}. In the Canadian Prairies over-drainage was a risk---15~m spacing promoted yield loss, 40~m being a threshold avoiding negatives \parencite{Cordeiro2015}---and in North Dakota narrower spacing suited wet years and wider spacing dry years and sugarbeet \parencite{Acharya2019}. In China deeper burial and closer spacing generally raised yield and desalination \parencite{Liu2025,Yang2022,Guo2025,Hou2018}, and a 0.3--1.5~m managed water table increased cane and sugar yield \parencite{CAMP1982}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Salt Leaching and Reclamation of Saline and Waterlogged Soils
claim_paragraph: Leaching is vertically stratified and ionically selective. Desalinization is strongest at the surface and weakens with depth (upper $>$ middle $>$ lower), with deeper layers sometimes resisting or reversing **[CITATION CHECKED: Narjary2024]**, modulated by texture (clayey sublayers limit leaching) \parencite{Qin2025}. Ion mobility follows characteristic sequences (Na$^+$ $>$ Cl$^-$ $>$ SO$_4^{2-}$ $>$ Mg$^{2+}$ under heavy rain \parencite{Yu2016}), with Cl and Na leached most efficiently (91\% and 88\% at 0--20~cm) and Ca persisting largely as precipitated gypsum \parencite{Qian2025,Sharma2000}. Re-accumulation is a frequent complication: seasonal dynamics follow a ``wash-out--recovery--accumulation'' pattern correlated with reproductive growth, some wide-spacing treatments showing secondary-salinization risk \parencite{Zhu2025b}, late-stage re-salinization can occur despite effective spring leaching (more severely under controlled than free drainage) \parencite{Dou2022}, and surface accumulation reappears in dry periods \parencite{Yu2016,Shi2021b}. Salinity around drains is spatially organised, with desalinization zones forming within about 0.0--0.3~m of the drain and low-salinity zones within about 5~m \parencite{Lu2019,Heng2021,Han2023,Mirlas2003,Benyamini2005}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Salt Leaching and Reclamation of Saline and Waterlogged Soils
claim_paragraph: Subsurface drainage reliably lowers the water table below the root zone and removes salt from the upper profile, converting saline and waterlogged land into productive cropland, with topsoil salinity reductions commonly 35--80\% and corresponding yield gains, validated at full production scale \parencite{Yang2025,Derby2024}. In the Northern Great Plains, tile-drained topsoil salinity declined while an undrained area did not, and soybean and corn yields improved within three years \parencite{Derby2024}. In India, drained-block salinity fell from 7.18 to 4.62~dS~m$^{-1}$ (35.7\% mean, 16.0--66.3\% range) while undrained rose, and yields rose 18.75--27.62\% \parencite{Sharma2006}; monsoon leaching brought weighted-average ECe to 1.4, 2.1, and 3.4~dS~m$^{-1}$ at 25, 50, and 75~m spacing \parencite{Sharma2000}; wide-spacing reclamation lowered topsoil salinity from 8.4 to about 2.1~dS~m$^{-1}$ and raised cropping intensity from 143\% to 191\% \parencite{Manjunatha2004}; and Tungabhadra evaluation reduced head- and middle-reach ECe from about 9 to 1.9--3.8~dS~m$^{-1}$ \parencite{Karegoudar2022}. Chinese reclamations are similarly large: pipe drainage cut 0--80~cm salinity from 35 to 15~g~kg$^{-1}$ versus 25--35 for open ditches \parencite{Wang2020}; drip-plus-pipe cut EC from 14.42--15.74 to 2.86--6.91~dS~m$^{-1}$ and raised seed cotton yield 52\% \parencite{Heng2021}; and after four years the 0--1.0~m layer fell from 27.6 to 4.1--7.2~dS~m$^{-1}$ \parencite{Zhang2021}. Desalinization is surface-concentrated: 0--20~cm rates exceeded 80\% while deeper layers lagged \parencite{Han2023}, and the meta-analysis found reduction greatest at $\leq$20~cm and nonsignificant below 80~cm \parencite{Yang2025}. Comparable reductions are reported for Turkey (topsoil about 80\% at 20~cm) \parencite{Bahçeci2009}, Tunisia (mean 23.3\%) \parencite{HajAmor2019}, and Canada (ECe 14.08 to 9.58~dS~m$^{-1}$, barley yield up to twentyfold) \parencite{Steppuhn2006,Steppuhn2017}. Reclamation homogenises the field (coefficient of variation 48.13\% to 28.14\%, 7~g~kg$^{-1}$ critical salinity) \parencite{Yu2015,Yu2025} and improves soil physical condition (porosity, infiltration 5.3 to 13.6--16.0~mm~h$^{-1}$, lower bulk density, SARe, ESP) **[CITATION CHECKED: Sharma2000]**. In Egypt drainage raised yields 13--16\% and farm income 9--44\% \parencite{Kotb2000}, whereas where the water table stays shallow, combined waterlogging and salinity are more damaging than waterlogging alone and yields fail above 12~dS~m$^{-1}$ \parencite{Kahlown2002}.

section: Drainage Management Outcomes and Viability
subsection: Nutrient and Sediment Loss Reductions and the Flow--Load Coupling
claim_paragraph: Denitrification is a secondary, well-documented pathway where the water table is held high: Canadian farm-scale work found greater relative abundance of nitrate-reducing bacteria under CD and reduced suspended solids and particulate phosphorus by damping macropore flow **[CITATION CHECKED: Tanga2025]**. Several syntheses caution that in poorly drained soils nitrate reduction is attributable mainly to reduced effluent rather than increased denitrification \parencite{THOMAS1995}, and Albanian data found system type barely affected concentrations, outflow volume being the dominant control \parencite{Grazhdani1996}. Belgian modeling reproduced an adverse relationship whereby wider spacings and higher water tables increase denitrification and reduce leaching but also reduce plant uptake, so total winter NO$_3$-N losses fall under CD \parencite{ElSadek2002,ElSadek2002b}. Phosphorus responses are generally favourable but smaller and occasionally reversed: CD lowered P loads in Sweden and Iran \parencite{Wesström2007,Wesström2001,Jouni2018}, yet North Carolina simulations found a small P efflux increase even as nitrate fell by up to 34\% \parencite{DEAL1986}, and Iranian data showed slightly higher P concentrations under CD though lower losses overall \parencite{Jouni2018}. Timing matters: autumn--winter is the most hazardous period, and P peaks can shift toward periods of highest outflow under CD \parencite{Tolomio2018,Wesström2007}. A recurring caveat is that CD may increase loss through seepage and surface runoff, partially offsetting drain-flow reductions \parencite{Frankenberger2024}.
